utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll go into closed session while the witness enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tanic. We are still with Mr. Fila, and I remind you that the solemn declaration continues to apply to your evidence. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And our agreement not to argue still holds.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm going to read the last quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've cut it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic writes in his book: "After returning to Belgrade, the minister is saying nothing. Mihajlovic a couple of months prior to that had asked him about his relationship with the SDB, disagreements with the service during the war on aggression. I told him as much as I could. He's an agent of a foreign service. He's also ours. He works for money. He's a bad person, and that I'm going to verify what happened during the war and aggression. I did verify, and I found out that he cheated during wartime. And if somebody cheats during wartime, then scores are settled in a different manner; there was kidnapping, et cetera." Mr. Tanic, you heard the opinion of Mr. Mijatovic, the one who you invoked as the main source of information, and that Jovica Stanisic used him to relay information to you. From what I heard, it transpires that you are just an associate, that you were unreliable, that you cheated, that you worked only for the money, et cetera; and this is -- these are his words. Will you agree with me, therefore, that you were just an ordinary collaborator of the state security, that you were unreliable and regular associates; just give information and never receive information?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you, but I'd like you to continue reading that paragraph. There are very interesting things concerning my kidnapping, which confirm everything I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It -- I read just a piece because it's not been translated. Everything is going to be translated, and the Bench will read everything. So what I wanted to hear is whether ordinary associate --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... That paragraph be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request that the rest of that paragraph be read. I can bring it up in re-direct, I understand, but it's such a long distance in time that I think it may lose it's essence if there's a day between knew and the time I'm able to address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure Mr. Fila will read it to accommodate you, as he says, but personally I would not have thought it was necessary. Because it appears to me that there's no dispute, but that Mr. Tanic was working in some capacity with the security service. And there's no dispute, as far as I'm aware at the moment, that he and his wife was subjected to some form of abduction. The real -- and we do waste a lot of time if we spend it on issues like that when the challenge is to his reliability, or the reliability of the material that he has provided. Now, if I'm wrong in assuming that that is the real range of the issue here, then I hope counsel will alert me to it. But that seems to be what the cross-examination is focusing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree with that, Your Honour. The one thing in this -- in the remaining sentences relates to the identity of the perpetrators of the kidnapping, which I think has some importance in -- for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Fila has indicated he'll oblige you. So could you give us the rest of the quotation, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I established another important thing. He was kidnapped by the members of the JSO. The same as they did when arresting Vlado Nikolic, former chief of analysis of the Belgrade centre."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot catch up with the overlap. The interpreter's note is that there is overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "So we are putting the pieces together, a small group of JSO members took part in the Ibar assassination attempt. Extortion, racketing ring. They didn't -- they are not interested in names, in legal grounds. They did what they did in arrest of the Bajic brothers. We've come closer to the murder of Slavko Curuvija and the disappearance of Ivan Stambolic. This task could have been maybe would have been brought to a close sooner, if my dearest minister would not have given so many statements at press conferences." Are you satisfied now, Mr. Tanic. I'm not disputing whether Mr. Tanic has been kidnapped or not or that he hasn't worked with the security service. Why I'm saying this is I want to dispute his ranking within the service. I want to demonstrate that he is not a James Bond type of operative, but a usual, ordinary associate or collaborator.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You will agree with me that ordinary associates just give information, never receive, and that they always have a pseudonym. Your pseudonym was Rabin, or rabbi in English. So if you are an ordinary associate, you could only provide information and not receive information from the service. Is that true? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. This is not correct because I was not an ordinary associate. If you followed closely, I said that over the past couple of years I've had no pseudonym or in the last couple of years in service I did not have a pseudonym. You can ask Mr. Mijatovic, and I have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, your microphone is not on and there is definitely an overlap occurring. You will need to observe the pause until the witness's answer is translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Highness, what I'm worried about is time. I read a paragraph from this book, and I wanted to seek and elicit his conclusions. And he is wasting my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know the English expression "the more hurry, the less speed." I don't know how that might translate into Serbian, but it is something to bear in mind, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have another proverb that's: "If you take a shortcut, you will get there later."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why would -- would an ordinary associate with a pseudonym only provide information or receive from the receive?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An ordinary associate just provides information. You know what the head of the Belgrade centre of the State Security Service does not personally pay ordinary associates. Mr. Mijatovic, on the previous page, said that he paid for me for my work. An ordinary associate would not be paid by the head of the service. Ordinary associates never see the head of the service, never sit down with the number two or number three in the service at the same table. Ordinary associates work with operatives, they are run by operatives, and paid by operatives. And the fact that Mr. Mijatovic said that he paid me belies his words. What he said about me being deceitful, then charges would have been brought and not -- I would have not been the kidnapped. And of course -- especially my wife. Parts of the JSO were Milosevic's death squadrons. JSO would be sent to special Milosevic's enemies, singled out as particularly dangerous by Milosevic himself. JSO would not be dealing with just ordinary people. Do you know how much it costs to kidnap me and my wife, to close down a whole block of streets, five to six vehicles, 20 people. Do you believe that such an expense would be wasted on an ordinary collaborator?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wanted to elicit your comment on Mr. Mijatovic's words, that Mijatovic -- Mihajlovic was trying to get information who you were. He said that you were unreliable, and you mentioned criminal responsibility, foreign agents are criminally prosecuted. And you were being betraying of your country pursuant to the 1992 Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, get a hold on. Mr. Fila, this is a massacre. With the British intelligence service, I did not engage in spying against Serbia, as I stated already. We were working on stymie-ing the belligerent conduct of Milosevic's regime. We were not dealing with espionage. All people who work with intelligence service do not deal with espionage exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You could not disclose state secrets because you did not possess them. You were just an ordinary agent of the SDB for the money. This is your main ideology; money. Mijatovic accused you of that, and this is the only inference that can be drawn from this. And the Serbian Criminal Code states that whoever works with a foreign intelligence service is a traitor and should be criminally prosecuted, during wartime especially. If you were working for the SDB, I can accept that. But if you work for a foreign intelligence service, then this is a crime.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why no criminal charges have been brought against me at any point, and that is an important point in the whole matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel. Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have my statement? Maybe the usher may help me get a copy of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The first paragraph of your statement, let us orientate what we are going to deal with. You say that your statement is based on three parts. Maybe I should let you read the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, go on, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You say that there are three bases to your statement. One is your personal experience in conducting discreet negotiations with Albanians, with the approval of Slobodan Milosevic in 1995/1997; your personal experience of -- in the spring of 1999 when I was a liaison officer with the western governments and Serbian government; and talks conducted through Zoran Mijatovic. And since you were deposed in 1999/2000, we are covering a period of 1995 and 2000.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone for counsel was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not going to deal with the first basis. The second, your claim that you are liaison officer between the western countries and Yugoslav government --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is lots of overlap, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, please. This can't go on, and there has to be some discipline exercised by both of you. You cannot talk over each other. And when one finishes, there has to be a time lapse before the other starts speaking because translation is not complete. You know that yourself, Mr. Tanic. When things are translated into your language, we have to wait while you hear the interpretations. It works for each language. So please focus the questions, Mr. Fila, perhaps a little more briefly; and please, Mr. Tanic, answer as briefly as you can. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've tried to cut it short, but I didn't have sufficient time to ask my question, so the question is based on just what I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That you were the liaison man on behalf of the Yugoslav government, and I emphasise that. You've never mentioned that over the last few days or, for that matter, in any of your statements. We are after all talking about the Yugoslav government. In which way were you authorised to do anything by the Yugoslav government? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation was not there yet. I had to wait for the interpretation to enter. Mr. Fila has failed to read the entire sentence. The Yugoslav government in a bid to find an honourable solution to put a stop to NATO's bombing campaign. So that's that. So that authority or those powers stem from the fact that I was on the way already towards helping find a solution to bring the war to an end. So it says I was the liaison man between the Yugoslav government and the western governments in a bid to find an honourable solution to put a stop to NATO's bombing campaign. That's all to easy to ascertain that I did indeed hold that position at a later stage in this trial. As a lot of things seem to be established about me at a pretty late stage, all I can say is I had the powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question is: Who on behalf of the Yugoslav government authorised you? The person you mentioned is someone altogether different. I'm talking about the Yugoslav government; it has a prime minister, deputy prime minister, members of the cabinet, and so on and so forth. Who authorised you on behalf of the Yugoslav government to do anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things I was setting out; I had not been authorised by the service only. It was through Mihajlovic that authorisation had been obtained through Milan Milutinovic, who was a member of the cabinet at the time I believe. He also authorised my journey, and through Mihajlovic he received a report on the peace offer. He made comments. He said that it was identical to the substance of his own talks with the foreign minister of another country, and this is easy enough to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please stop him. I don't have time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What will you say if I tell you this: Neither Dusan Mihajlovic nor Milutinovic were cabinet members at the time under consideration?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment to make. The Yugoslav government, the very phrase, was used in a way that simply -- what could you possibly say? Between Milosevic's regime, the Yugoslav government, Belgrade, and the west, all these are political phrases that mean next to nothing. The essence of the matter is: I was there. People in power knew that I was on my way there. I came back with a result. I described the result as I described it a while ago. It wasn't there in any book for me to read about. Milosevic and Milutinovic were informed as well as the security service. It wasn't until after two years after my evidence that this book emerged that Lilic has something to do with that as well, and he came back with the same result. This is not a fabrication on my part; that would have been impossible. That's should be easy enough to ascertain. I certainly had not been authorised by, I don't know, somebody like my own aunt or uncle. You see my point. I got the money for that journey. I was authorised to leave by the Crisis Staff, and there you have it. There was a perfectly valid report about that offered, too. The one thing that is slightly improper about that, or not quite correct, I was one of the people liaising between the Yugoslav government and the western countries in order to reach an honourable solution, but I did not know who the others involved were so I do not wish to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. So we agree that you were never authorised by the Yugoslav government to do anything, were you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We definitely have not agreed on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the sort of question that really doesn't help us because the witness has given an answer. We know that his view of what might be government authorisation is not the same as the proposition you're advancing to him. And we will sort that out in due course, but we know that the two of you will never agree on -- in these sort of general propositions. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You talked about submitting a report. Do you still keep a copy of that report for your own purposes?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A copy of that report, my god, Mr. Fila. Mr. Mihajlovic has a copy in his files, if I remember correctly; he's the one you should go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's move on to something else. At one point you said that you received your authority for negotiations from three different sources, and the fact was there was no democracy in the government. If there was no democracy in the government, you will agree with me that you no longer had the authority or the powers. Is that true? Or the New Democratic Party, rather, was no longer in the government.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the question because the microphone was switched off halfway through the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, your question has been omitted -- hasn't been picked up by the interpreters because the microphone wasn't turned on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, he says that the authority for the negotiations came from three different sources; one of them being the fact that the New Democracy party was a member of the government. I asked him whether that authority ceased when the New Democratic Party left the government, and the witness's answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just clarify what negotiations we're talking about, with the Albanians or to end the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear, physically hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, what you've said has not been heard. It may be to do with the microphone, but you've then had a quick exchange with the witness which hasn't been picked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12, the fact that New Democracy was no longer in government; page 12, line 8, that's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we've got that, but something else has been said -- anyway, please move on to your next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 10, you talk about institutional links. You say you met Zoran Mijatovic once; and during your examination-in-chief on the 10th of October, on page 6275, lines 19 through 24, you say that you met a man whose name was mentioned in closed session and Mijatovic whenever necessary, and it went on like that until October 1998. What do you mean by "institutional links?"

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says communication between institutions or inter-institutional communication and not links. Now, these are two different things, are they? At least in our language. The concept of inter-institutional communication in the life of an intelligence community implies a series of actions determine -- used to determine the level of a meeting, the degree of urgency involved, the nature of any subjects to be raised; will a meeting be recorded or not, will it just be a verbal meeting, will an associate just simply make a statement, or will they be -- will there be counter-intelligence involved or any possible feedback; will anything be written down, what about the person receiving this information, will they write anything down? This is what I mean when I say communications between institutions. For example, I say there is a problem. It's not a major problem. All right, okay. See you next Sunday. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... This is a sufficient answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If you look at the next paragraph, you say you drafted written reports together with other persons from the State Security Service. Which other persons are you talking about? Which other persons are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's reference here to a person we're not supposed to mention, first and foremost. When I say we drafted written reports, you know it's a method we use in the security services. And I suppose I'm allowed to say that in open session. There you put together a report in the form of a journalistic piece or a newspaper article, and that's how you then proceed. I suppose that I'm allowed to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question is: What about these other persons from the State Security Services? Who are these other persons?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 11, and it's the last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Written analysis, in the course of my task, was produced in cooperation with members of the SDB. Who were these other members, and where did you produce these written analyses?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, the counsel is again trying to confuse the Chamber. Mijatovic is not a person that I worked with in drafting these reports, and then it goes on to state other persons. Well, these other persons are persons who have been mentioned before. Operatives mentioned previously in closed session. So these are your other persons. Before, we were speaking about Mijatovic. These reports were normally produced on official premises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please confine the answer. You've answered the question. Now, let's move to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 15, you say that Slobodan Milosevic approved of your work. Based on your statement, I see that these are round-table negotiations in actual fact. When you say negotiations, you mean round-table discussions. You claim that Milosevic approved the results reached by one such round-table discussion, in order for you to participate in another such discussion. Is that what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, Mr. Fila. Again, the Defence is trying to exaggerate and twist the meaning of something. There were NGO groups and there were round-table discussions in order to have the participation of a third party, without the third party necessarily being a country. I provided a very specific definition of that, explanation of that. It wasn't just one single NGO; there were several rounds of round-table discussions, closed and semi-closed. These were used as an opportunity for persons to meet after official meetings and to informally participate. There was Agani participating in this round-table discussion and Mr. Perisic as a representative of the SPS. It was in the Sava centre, where I was back in 1995. It was at the time that Mr. Perisic was a high ranking official of the SPS. For example, should they have deemed it necessary, they would have had an opportunity to sit down together and talk for ten or 15 minutes in full secrecy. This was merely a smoke-screen, a well-meaning smoke-screen for negotiations to be brought to a successful conclusion. I employed this method just like all the other people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked you a question and you provided an answer. You said: Yes. Well, that's that.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but my answer was not yes. If you will please excuse me, my answer was definitely not yes. There were a whole succession of meetings, one third of which were round-table debates, or at least a half. There was a group of intellectuals there, and you know that full well, Fila. I'm not sure why you're asking me that, because you know that all to well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's because I looked at your statement. You participated in three round-table debates up until 1997. New Democracy was not in government at the time. After that there were no round-table, no institutional links, no inter-institutional communications or meetings with Slobodan Milosevic for that matter after 1997. That's what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Well, we have to wait for the interpretation to finish. What shall we do, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: The microphone was not on. We didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer to your question was no. You are simply not right; pure and simple. You should call some experts on politics, and then you will see what the methodology behind this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In 22, you said that the Albanians accepted the first stage of negotiations, measures for mutual confidence building, and this was supposed to take two years. Are these the two years that were raised in examination-in-chief and suddenly grew out of proportion and became a 15-year period, and when exactly did any Albanians accept that, and which Albanians specifically?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, all right. This is not the 15 years that were mentioned before. In my statement I was clear. I said this was stage one of confidence building, and the implementation took roughly two years. Agani agreed when we were in Pristina sometime in 1995, possibly 1996. He agreed on principle with these policies to take it step by step. It wasn't just me being there advocating these policies. Mr. Paglia can confirm that for your benefit. He was there on behalf of the contact group, and his information is very similar. We cross-referenced our information in preparation for my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You say that they accepted to go back to autonomy. When did the Albanians accept that? When?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in 1996. They were facing a severe crisis, a political crisis. All the western countries at the time were backing Belgrade's policies. We were talking about full autonomy, about essential autonomy, not autonomy as defined back in 1986. Since they realised that the western governments or the international community did not back their requests, claims, and since they realised that everybody was backing Belgrade's policy, they withdrew to some extent from their previous position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Listen. I'm trying to answer your question. What I'm asking you is when and which Albanians? Did they agree to this in writing? Is there anything you have to show for this?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't agree in writing, Mr. Fila. These were secret negotiations. They agreed in principle to not drag their feet, and you can see that if you look at the newer declaration, where it says without prejudicing the eventual solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, who were the Albanians who agreed in principle to accept Milosevic's offer of a return to autonomy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Fehmi Agani, Rugova's deputy and envoy. In the 1960s, in Pristina, we had two meetings. We had meetings about these confidence-building measures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Names are all I want at the moment. Apart from Agani, who else was involved in that agreement or acceptance in principle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody else. Nobody else could possibly have accepted that or refused. Agani was -- you know, Rugova was in power, and Agani was his envoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the other matter I want to be clear about is you talk about return to autonomy; and then you now try to expand that concept to something called full autonomy, which I have to say causes confusion in my mind. What is meant by this expression "autonomy"? Does that mean that Kosovo would be a republic, or does it mean something short of that that you can define, or does it mean something nebulous that you can't define?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It doesn't mean a republic, but we used to refer it to the concept as autonomy-plus; less than a full republic, but more than full autonomy. This would have presented problems later for constitutional experts. I was paving the way to a political solution, and I'm no constitutional expert. In the sense of politics, we called it or we thought about it more than autonomy, but less than a republic. Autonomy-plus. I can describe it if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you just describe the "plus" element to me, then that might help. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is some explanation that in paragraph 16 of his statement, which is in evidence. On page 4 about four lines up from the bottom, there's a reference to what the "plus" referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no mention of Albanians accepting it; that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? In 1996, the Albanian side was in a very serious position vis-a-vis Belgrade, and this is the vital part of my testimony, if I may. Milosevic enjoyed the positive spin-offs after the Dayton Agreement, because everyone expected that he would present a constructive factor as he had promised at the Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, we've already heard this.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did you hear this, Mr. Fila? That's the essence of this tragedy of ours. We held the political victory in our hands pertaining to Kosovo, and Milosevic just destroyed it. When did you hear this? He turned the Albanian terrorists into freedom fighters; have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop. Mr. Fila, ask another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraphs 31 and 32, you talk about foreign diplomatic efforts to achieve peace. Did you know that there was a summit in Crete of the countries of the Balkans region, and Fatosh Nano and Milosevic met on that occasion. That was a first meeting of Serbian and Albanian president since 1946. And Fatosh Nano said Kosovo was an internal Serbian affair. I'm interested why the summit was not mentioned; this effort invested by the regime to get peace. There's no mention of it. Did you know that a summit took place?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know about it. I've been telling you that Milosevic participated in the negotiations as well, and you didn't believe me. I wasn't there; that's why I didn't mention it. I knew of it, but I also knew that what was arranged there was not implemented. We, on the other hand, met with the Albanians. I met with the Albanian minister of the interior during that meeting. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned Predrag Simic and his book wrote to Rambouillet. I believe you've read it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember that it was his assessment that the increase in activities of the KLA in Kosovo was a reaction to the Crete agreement. Because the KLA saw it as their last chance to fight and to do away with any peaceful efforts. This is also in the book.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Fila's microphone was switched off for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The assessment is very interesting. I know Mr. Simic very well. He's an intellectual, and I advise you to write -- read the book and what he wrote about me. It is partially correct. I agree. The only problem is that Milosevic, as you can read from Stanisic's statements, would not allow our organs, our bodies to deal with the KLA by way of arrests or simply doing away with the entire organisation. He allowed the KLA to grow, and the problem was that there were conflicts at the time already. And if you look at the table, you will see that the increase of Albanian terrorism began as of that moment when Milosevic started protecting Kosovo. But I agree with the assessment. It is rather important, and it is not contradictory to what I'm saying. Mr. Simic put it rather well. The only problem was that the KLA had already been in existence. You should read what Stanisic said at page 239 of Mijatovic's book, page 239 of Mijatovic's book. Stanisic's opinion of Kosovo in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Tanic, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the same book it is stated that Fehmi Agani did not accept, or rather, gave up on Bertelsmann Foundation's recommendation? This is in the same book and concerns Mr. Agani. Do you remember that? I guess you were there.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the meeting. It was nice of you to refresh my memory. It was another situation which I was there with Mr. Agani and western diplomats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please answer the question, would you? Do you remember that in the same book it is stated that Agani did not accept, or rather, gave up on Bertelsmann Foundation's recommendations? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, since he only gave up partially. He was going from one side to another. He changed position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, paragraph 32, you mention a document, a paper. You state that the Albanians gave up on independence. Did you know that Mr. Rugova, in Belgrade, refused to reject independence? There was no one on the Albanian side at that time or nowadays to give up on the notion of independence. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now there aren't any, but at that time they were ready -- they were not ready to give up independence completely. I wanted to say that they were willing to put the issue of independence within a longer historical context, to see what comes out of it. Of course, the final goal was not to give up on it completely, although you can interpret it as such. But if someone says, "Let's drop it for the next ten or 15 years," then that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Paragraph 35, you talk about Milosevic's speech in Pristina on the 25th of June, 1997, in negative light. During your cross-examination, Milosevic read parts of the speech to you on page 5081, lines 2 through 17, the date 16th of May, 2000. I wasn't going to read this to you to save time, but I wanted to ask you this: Did you in the meantime re-read the speech. Can you tell us where in the speech can we find what you assert? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recall, he put it clearly in that speech that Kosovo was an integral part of Serbia. He didn't mention Yugoslavia but Serbia. I can go through the speech again. I may have omitted a thing or two; but as far as I know, this speech was not exactly in keeping with the results of the negotiations until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We can see the transcript for ourselves, and should you need to see the entire speech I am willing to give it to you.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be happy to see it. Perhaps later you can give it to me so that I can read it back in my hotel room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the speech an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wanted to use it to see whether his memory is any better than in 2002, whether he re-read it in the meantime. If he didn't, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, if there are points to be made about the inaccuracy of the comments in paragraph 35, then these are comments that can be made in submissions if the Chamber had the speech in addition, of course, to the transcript, which we do have. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you do have the transcript, Your Honour, but I would indicate that it appears from the transcript, at page 5081, Mr. Milosevic reads out parts of the speech, but he apparently doesn't read the whole speech because at line 8 he says: "Now I'm going to skip a part," and then it says "thus and so." So it appears the whole speech was not put to the witness at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it would nevertheless make sense for us to have the whole speech, so we can put the comments in context. But we don't need to go over the speech here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be translated, and you will receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 28, you state that in September 1997 a document was created by the name of "Joint Recommendations." It is Exhibit P0 -- P2481. This is based on the recommendations you made to Milosevic at the meeting you had with him and some other people back in 1995. This document dates back to September 1997. How is it possible that Milosevic in his speech from June 1997 annulled something which was created only three months subsequently, as you state in paragraph 35?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're trying to abuse the political processes in order to confuse the Board. You are mentioning Agani, Milosevic, Rugova, this and that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, just answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milosevic did, as Agani and Rugova and others during the negotiations. Maybe I should have said a signal was given to annul the results of the negotiations, then he went to Crete, and then he changed his mind again. We know what the nature of that regime was; one week one thing, the next week the other thing. Mr. Fila, as if you don't know what the regime was like. In the next six months, well, Milosevic would negotiate, and then he wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just asked him how Milosevic was able to prevent in June something which took place in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I mean it -- when a witness has difficulty answering a specific question like that, often a witness will resort to aggression rather than simply answering the question. And the Court might form the impression that that's what the witness has just done. When he then concentrates on the question, he gives an answer that's plausible. And we would then have to work our way through it. But situation is complicated for us by the fact that the witness takes this aggressive attitude to your question, which is rather unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I perhaps used the wrong words. Perhaps I should have said he gave a negative signal in his speech in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Let's drop it. Mr. Tanic, you are talking about the meeting in New York from where Mihajlovic allegedly brought that piece of paper, the one we discussed. I wanted to ask you this, and I would kindly ask for an answer: Did you know that that meeting in New York was actually a gathering of individuals under the auspices of the forum for inter-ethnic relations, where around the round-table the participants exchanged views on current topics? No one was authorised to carry out any negotiations and Vesna Pesic was there on behalf of the Citizens' Council as well as Vuk Draskovic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, it was a round-table discussion. Agani was there and the representative from Madeleine Albright's cabinet. Just look at list of participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked you this: Was this organised by the forum for inter-ethnic relations and that people were there as individuals? That forum is from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even formally. The forum was one of the organiser. The other organiser was one of the foundations of the state department, but it was in the form of a round-table discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 36, you mention an expression of jointly accepted or agreed positions. This is the paper we were referring to, but you never mentioned where you find that Rugova gave up on independence. Where is that? Can you show it to the Bench already?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rugova never did it in writing. These were secret negotiations. There was change of positions, negotiations, trying to outplay the other. But I categorically state that Rugova and Agani were prepared to postpone the issue of independence; whereas, on our part, we saw our window of opportunity to join the EU in the meantime. And then the Albanians would be allowed to secede if they wanted to. But at -- you're trying to say that they gave up on it at that time. They never did. The politics is about winning and losing at a particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anyone say that orally, that we can check, because in paragraph 36 you say: "Ibrahim Rugova, the president of the Kosovar Albanians, accepted to give up on the notion of independence."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "secession."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Fila's microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said he didn't put it in writing. How about using the words where, with whom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the secret negotiations with Monsignor Paglia, he was there on behalf of the contact group. Then he practically said that the issue of secession and independence can be postponed. Well, you know, just concessions are difficult to gain or give. The Albanian side waited on -- for Milosevic to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that Rugova never gave up on it, be it in writing or orally, as what may have or may not have taken place in subsequent negotiations, that's another issue?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask for a clarification about he never gave up on "it," because Mr. Fila's question on page 27, line 13, was, "did Ibrahim Rugova say the Albanians accepted to give up on the notion of independence." In paragraph 36, what is stated in the English is that, "Ibrahim Rugova, the president of the Kosovar Albanians, had agreed to step back from secession." I would say those are two slightly different things, and I think the witness needs to be clear what the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness answered the last question by saying that he practically said that the issue of secession and independence can be postponed. So I would assume the witness views these as the same, and Mr. Fila then asked the question: Do you agree with me that Rugova never gave up on it. Is it not just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- a question of two words for the same concept, basically? So please answer the question, Mr. Tanic. The question was: Do you agree with Mr. Fila that Rugova never gave up on secession, independence; whatever you wish to call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did he give up on that, in writing or orally, that he stood up and said, "We are giving up on independence," when and where?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? This part of the testimony can create further chaos down there in the region and can bring about further dithering and can bring some people in Kosovo into a disadvantaged situation. So I propose that we move into private or closed session with the Court's pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There's no reason for going into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. That would not be an appropriate reason for us to hear evidence in private session. The -- there are two issues here. You've said that Monsignor Paglia was present when this was indicated. Now, can you be more specific about what indication was given by Rugova of his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he indicated this: Of course, for the Albanian people, the notion of independence remains a permanent political goal. However, because of the objective state of play and the circumstances obtaining and the interest for the Albanians for this matter to be started resolved -- being resolved and by political means, they would accept a step-by-step approach. First, four or five measures to build confidence over two years; and then a temporary status of Kosovo, which would imply a restoration of full autonomy, autonomy-plus. That would be lasting for a longer period of time. Subsequently, at Rambouillet, they cut that short. And asked not only by Monsignor Paglia, but you can verify that with the state department and foreign office. When Rugova was asked: What about independence? A formula agreed by Agani and me in Pristina was applied for the notion of independence to remain a permanent political goal that the Albanians are going to fight for sometime in the future, and then in the meantime we are going to resolve this problem and conclude a political solution. That was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you refer to the foreign office, do you mean the United Kingdom foreign office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you have to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember where this happened, and roughly when it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot pin-point the date, the time, because this was a process where some headway was being made. This is a period between 1995 and 1996, that period, particularly 1996, immediately after the Dayton Accords. Let's put it in 1996. This -- it was a series of talks. This is no secret. I would like to highlight this formulation. It remains their permanent political goal, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. Now, Mr. Fila, bearing in mind that there seem to be no absolutes in this trial, you've perhaps got the answer, the only answer, you're going to get to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot accept anything more, obviously. I'm going to bring my cross to a close soon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. Fila. If I may describe this. They were sitting back and waiting for Milosevic to make a mistake --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Yourself and confine yourself to answering questions. Once your answer is complete, leave it at that and we'll move to another question. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The only thing I'd like to hear more about now is that you mentioned a helicopter that Perisic and Stanisic took to travel to Kosovo. I would like to ask you to explain that why this helicopter is never mentioned in your earlier statements, sir. You haven't mentioned it to the OTP in your additional interview. Now this helicopter springs up here. I put it to you that this helicopter flight never took place, that Sainovic, Perisic, and Stanisic never took together a helicopter to fly there. Think about it. I believe that your memory was much better in 2002.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was told to me by Perisic. Initially, I did not this take as an important fact; it was just an illustration of theirs that they could not work with Sainovic. It was told to me by Perisic. It's just an illustration. It is not pertinent to the subject matter at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, another thing is interesting to me. You said that the main thesis of your book was that Milosevic intentionally provoked the war with NATO. The question I'm interested in is whether you received that 5.000 euro from the British intelligence service because of that claim in your future book.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My main thesis was that Milosevic intentionally provoked the war with Kosovo Albanians in Kosovo, and after that with NATO. I did not receive 5.000 euro from the Brits because of this thesis, but to cover my expenses. I had to travel to check and double-check with international factors some of my thesis to see whether I'm in the right or not, and it costs money. My thesis was that Milosevic intentionally provoked war in Kosovo and that he turned Albanian terrorists into freedom fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the Brits ask you to give the money back, since you did not write the book eventually? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone was off for counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that question appears to have been answered. Unless you have some particular foundation for suggesting that that payment was an advance for a book, then I would not be prepared to allow you to pursue this. But have you a basis for saying that or have I misunderstood the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. In a previous statement he said that he proved Serbian victims, and the British service was interested in giving him money for the publication of the book and that he would receive money from them for the purpose of writing the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you are going to agree, Witness, to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have a reference to where that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, can we?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me find it. Paragraph 2 states about the content of the book. Can we resolve it in a simple manner. Can I ask the witness whether the Brits gave him the money to write the book? I cannot find the place, but there is such a claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, is it true that you received 10.000 German marks on two occasions connected with your writing the book, that was the basis for your receiving the money?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to the costs related to the writing of the book, and the Brits were interested in Serb victims, crimes perpetrated by the Haradinaj brothers, and you may ask Mr. Mijatovic about the origins. You know, you will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So my question: If you did not write this book, did the British secret service ask you to give the money back? I believe that the UK is a wealthy country, but ...

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very difficult question to answer -- well, the book has been written, so don't worry about that. And one day, if I will be in a position to publish it, it will be published.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you another thing, and this is going to conclude my examination. You said that Milosevic had absolute control over the security services, MUP, and the military answering a question by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you pin-point that part of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: 6333, lines 6 to 8.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was true particularly after Stanisic and Perisic had been removed. And he had control beforehand; but after Perisic and Stanisic were dismissed, he had absolute control over the security services and the military. And this is why they were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If he had such level of control as you claim - I may agree with you - why would he need a parallel line of command or chain of command when you say that everybody was doing their bidding? At some places you allude to orders being given to General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this beautiful question. He needed a parallel chain of command because he could not secure political control, neither in the federal parliament nor in the republican government, as you know. Federal parliament comprised Serbia and Montenegro, and the Serbian parliament comprised opposition as well. And in Serbia and Montenegro there were many people in parliament and in government who -- well, who knew that a political solution to the Kosovo problem was possible, however lame, so that Milosevic could not secure political control of the republican parliament and government and federal parliament and government. And this is why he established this parallel chain of command, otherwise he would not have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel repeat the question because of overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this would go for a political chain of command, not a police or military chain of command over which he usually had control, as you stated, to circumvent the parliament?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not some political control; it goes for constitutional political control through both parliaments and through the republican government and the republican Assembly and other --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, Mr. Fila. I regret, I don't understand the answer to the question. Why would these political grounds require him to have a parallel command structure or chain of command over the MUP, the security service, and the military, if he was effectively in control of all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, at that time Milosevic was president of Yugoslavia, let me remind you. So as Yugoslav president, he had very little authority and powers to conduct such affairs. The Serbian president was Milan Milutinovic. And constitutionally, he had much greater powers than Milosevic -- well, on paper, not de facto. And also while he was president of Serbia, Milosevic took the position of Yugoslav and Serb president in turns. He had de facto control, but he could not enact his decisions through parliament or through government, because he could not confine in everybody because then a riot would ensue and this is why he made this parallel chain of command. Had Milosevic, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only detailed evidence we've had about a parallel chain of command I think related to the army, if I'm not mistaken, and the army is a federal institution here. Now, why would he in relation to a federal institution need to have a parallel chain of command if he was legally and factually in control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, to use the military against the civilians in a part of the territory, pursuant to our allow, it is disallowed to use military against civilians. This is possible only in extraordinary circumstances, and for -- to introduce this state in Kosovo Milosevic had to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But your whole point is that he did do that. And the only reason, on the face of it, for requiring a parallel structure would be if there were intervening senior commanders in the army who would not implement apparently illegal orders. And the question you're being asked is: Once Perisic had gone, what was the obstruction to simply ordering this through the normal channels? Who was there to prevent Milosevic simply committing criminal acts if he wished through ordering them to be done by the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were, in the military, people who did not want to -- so in political structures in federal and republic governments, who disproved of that. But it is a fact that the parallel chain of command involved both the MUP; security services, after the removal of Jovica Stanisic; and the army. All these institutions were placed under the parallel chain of command through that commission, the federal commission for Kosovo, which changed its title subsequently. But in political structures, there were enough individuals who would oppose that had he used the institutional channel. This is my explanation as a politician. If you need a constitutional expert, you may --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I would like to say to intervene with regard to transcript page 31, lines 18, 21, the witness said that maybe this helicopter flight never took place. I would like this to be put on record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to that flight by Perisic, Stanisic, and Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, in relation to the helicopter flight, was one of the comments you made in answer that for all you know it may not have taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was told by Perisic, so I wasn't there myself. I didn't see the helicopter take off. It is just an assumption. Perhaps it did; perhaps it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the point. Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic, and I have a number of questions for you. I want to begin by reminding you of an answer you gave yesterday to a question by Mr. O'Sullivan. This is at page 38, line 23 of yesterday's transcript. You said to Mr. O'Sullivan this language: "Not correct. And this attorney-at-law is not qualified and does not have the expertise to interpret complicated political arrangements. It's simply incorrect. I was not going into armed forces technicalities. Could the counsel please be asked not a meddle with high politics and agreements." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, Mr. O'Sullivan failed to introduce himself as someone who is experienced in that sort of thing. And one thing that his questions indicated is that he was entirely untrained in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Well, let me tell you something right now. I want you to answer my questions and that's it. If you start making a speech, I'm going to stop you because you're doing it to keep me from answering all my questions. I know that's your tack here, and I'm not going to let you do it. I'll ask a question, you give an answer, and that will be it. Now, I will tell you, because you're claiming that Mr. O'Sullivan didn't, I will tell you that I have a degree in international affairs, which you don't; that I served in intelligence of United States army, which you didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object testify to this. He's testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think your objection is well founded, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Ackerman, you draw attention to a statement made yesterday which was inappropriate. It's for the Bench to decide just how to deal with these as we go along. Some of them are tackled face-on. Others are allowed just to go unanswered because the situation doesn't demand it. I was tempted at the stage that comment was made yesterday to make the point to the witness that the qualifications of counsel in anything other than the law are entirely irrelevant to the issues in the trial. Counsel is there properly briefed by appropriate experts to ask questions, and it's not for the witness to question the capacity of counsel. I decided not to do so. I didn't realise it was such a big issue. I thought Mr. O'Sullivan was comfortable with the situation. But I hope I've now made it clear to the witness that that is the role counsel plays. And I think with that indication you can proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a few moments ago there was some discussion, Mr. Tanic, about your book. And the Judge even raised some question about that. At page 52, line 14, yesterday you were being asked about that. And you said with regard to the amount of money: "I believe that it was 10.000 German marks. Today's counter value of 5.000 euro. For the expenses connected with the preparation of different materials, the book, et cetera." Can you tell me what else besides the book you were being paid for by the British intelligence people. What else were they compensating you for besides your work on this book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the book and everything in relation to the book. Travel expenses, I had to travel to Rome to see Mr. Paglia. I had to go to two or three other countries to see diplomats there to check my theories. In answer to your question, I wasn't paid for anything else by the British security services, apart from any expenses incurred during the writing of my book. After my exile, some of my living expenses were covered, but I was not in the pay of the British intelligence services, if that's what you were implying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were being paid, you claim now, a fee for writing the book, plus expenses for travel and things of that nature. How much was the fee for writing the book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My fee was zero. It was all about expenses that went towards the making of that book, travel expenses --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, all right --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then why did you say yesterday that it was for expenses connected with the preparation of different materials, the book, and so forth? So things other than the book. What other expenses were you being compensated for besides the writing of this book? Were you being paid for information?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say you worked with the US intelligence services. You know that this is not the fee that is normally paid for that sort of information, 100 German mark. It's not like they paid my coffee or anything. Whatever expenses were paid had to do with my book. Don't try to take every single word I say and twist it around to mean something else. I did not have a fee that was paid to me for any intelligence activity that I carried out. It would have been a much higher fee had there been one to begin with. You say you worked with the US intelligence. If indeed you worked for the US intelligence, you should know better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were privy to -- you claim you were privy to a great deal of secret information from your government. It's the case, isn't it, that you were providing secret information without the knowledge of your government to western intelligence agencies, and that that's why you were arrested as a possible spy, rather than being kidnapped as you claim. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never submitted any sort of intelligence to any foreign government, intelligence about Serbia or about Yugoslavia. It's true, we did exchange information. I did submit to them information that might have helped them to suppress Milosevic's belligerent behaviour. I was never arrested. I was kidnapped. Please stop these fabrications. If I had been a spy in someone's pay during the war, charges would have been brought against me. I would have been locked up in a prison. I wouldn't have been able to leave the country. Please don't insinuate. The deputy head of the intelligence service confirms for your benefit that indeed I was kidnapped, and now you say I was arrested as a spy. There's no such thing as a special spy. You are either a spy or you are not a spy. Not everyone who is authorised to do their work is a spy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tanic. Thank you. Now, we will have to break at this stage for 20 minutes. We'll go into closed session while Mr. Tanic leaves the court, and we'll remain that way until he returns.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've got one maybe final question regarding the book. You told us the first day you testified here that you had not published the book because in the witness protection programme, you're not entitled to publish anything. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not entitled to any form of public life at all, especially not of a political journalistic nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you say you're not entitled to publish anything, is there a rule that you can't submit your book for publication? Why does that interfere with anything?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness protection programme implies a change of identity and the removal of anything from one's previous life that might be used to identify this person. Publication of that book in this particular case would be contrary to the provisions of the witness protection programme; that much is certain. There's actually a document you sign when you become part of this programme that you will not be involved in any sort of activity that might be used to reveal your previous real identity. Publishing a book would certainly constitute one such infraction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if a book were to come out with your name on it, you think that would somehow compromise you in the witness protection programme? And if that's your belief, then how is it you're testifying here under the name Ratomir Tanic doesn't do the same thing? That makes no sense to me, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, this is a complex issue that I have to say I don't think exploration here will assist. It seems to me basic common sense that someone in a witness protection scheme should not be involved in the publication of a book, and also basic common sense that a country involved in the scheme would have such a requirement, to ensure that the steps they have to take are not compromised in any way by the publication openly of such material and the interest that might then be shown in the individual as a result. Testifying here can be viewed in a number of ways; and it's, some people might say, an obligation. It's quite different from the publication of a book. Is it reasonable to explore this; and secondly, will it advance a knowledge of matters in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think so. And I'm relying totally on memory, but I'm quite certain that mafia guy. Sammy "The Bull" Gravano published a book while he was in the protection programme. I don't think there's any prohibition against it. I think there's another reason for not getting the book published. I think it has to do with libel law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Different countries no doubt have different rules and different terms that they agree with people and that -- exploring that alone doesn't seem to me to be in the public interest or the interest of the witness. But if you wish to put a specific question about an ulterior motive, then that's perfectly proper..

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, one thing I hope I've learned in my career is that when the finders of the fact are not interested in what I'm doing, it's probably something I should not be doing. So I'll go on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I don't think you should doubt that. With permission, I'll say please do ask. Don't doubt, because this is just as things go on, and we keep understanding each other and appreciating points of views.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour. I will ask one further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was there ever a time when your manuscript was submitted to a publisher?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time the manuscript was completed I was already part of the witness protection programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to go on to something else, and this is just an effort to understand your view of your statement, which as -- part of which has been put in evidence in this case. In the Milosevic trial, at page 5108, line 6, you were being asked questions by Mr. Milosevic and he said: "You say there was a delegation, but here it says that there was you and Dusan Mihajlovic and not a delegation. When were you telling the truth; then or now?" The answer you gave is this: It's unfair. Once again it's a verbal trick to abuse the free interpretation of the working version." Now, first of all, what are you talking about when you're talking about the "working version?"

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, let me tell you one thing. Whenever you go to a meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, don't tell me one thing. Answer my question. What do you mean when you say "working version?"

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case I must tell you, I fail to understand your question. Can you please provide further clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll ask it again. You said in answer to Mr. Milosevic, who was asking you about your statement: "It's a verbal trick to abuse the free interpretation of the working version; "working version" referring to your statement. What do you mean by "working version?"

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, all right. Now I understand, and thank you for this clarification. The draft version of my statement, since he was using several different versions of my statement. So the draft version was the one that was used to set up a framework for this problem. At a later stage, things are further defined in a way more amenable to the purposes of a Court or the general public, something that you can freely use. In a draft version, sometimes you phrase things more liberally, which I did in relation to this meeting. Because Mihajlovic and I were the only two people briefing him, the important thing is who is doing the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Thank you. We don't need another speech. Now, first of all it's not true that Mr. Milosevic was using several versions of your statement. He had one version of your statement just like we have one version of your statement. If there are other versions of your statement, the Prosecutor has not given them to us, which would be a violation of the Rules. And I know that have not violated the rules in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour I have no other version of the statement than the one we provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the statement we have before us today, right at the very top, says draft statement of witness Tony X. And you told us, in answer to questions by Mr. Hannis, other than the changes you made that were submitted to us in a supplemental information sheet, everything in there was true and correct, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so when you said to Mr. Milosevic that him asking you about that statement was a verbal trick to abuse the free interpretation of the working version, what you were trying to do was say, "Please let me answer your question any way I want to, because my statement really isn't true." And he was tricking you by referring to this statement you've now sworn is true, right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'm saying is Milosevic employed a verbal ruse, a trick, if you allow me to quote your exact words. He knows that the main participants at that meeting were those doing the meeting and not those simply sitting pretty. When I gave my statement I wasn't being precise enough to be specific about that. There were several people at the meeting, but they weren't the ones briefing Milosevic. Milosevic wasn't talking to them. It was just Mihajlovic and myself, the only two people I specified. I didn't deem it necessary to mention anybody else who was there. This may have been an error on my part, for which I apologise. That changes nothing about the substance of that briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
