utterances.text: I want to go through an exercise now with you that I hope will not be too tedious, and I need your cooperation to try and make it as painless as possible for us to get through this. I think you have a copy of your statement in front of you. I'm going to try to refer very rapidly to a number of paragraphs and ask you just a very simple question. And I'm going to start with paragraph 5. And in paragraph 5 the sentence appears: "I know from my contacts with members of the SDB." With regard to that particular paragraph, who were the contacts that you had that you learned this from? Names, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't see that quote in paragraph 5. If I could please have the same statement that Mr. Ackerman is using. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have it, Mr. Tanic, and it's the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, all right. Yes. That is right after the one that was challenged. I understand. Well, yes, I've named my contacts already, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you say so, I accept that. Let's go to paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's important here to identify any paragraph or any comment made, Mr. Tanic, about an SDB contact, where that contact in fact is a person that you're not prepared to identify. So if in paragraph 5 the reference to "my contacts with members of the SDB" refers to someone you're not prepared to identify, you should tell us that. It may be that in that paragraph it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are identified in paragraph 5; the names are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the names that are there are those with whom you had perhaps the greatest contact. You say "especially," but that presupposes that you had contacts with more than simply the two named.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true. When I say "especially," that refers to the peculiar relevance of the information shared and not to any technical aspects of that situation. There were several contacts, but we can stay with this first name that was mentioned in closed session. He was an operative who monitored all of this at the intelligence level. Obviously, it wasn't the head of the service who monitored things at an intelligence level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Ackerman wants to take you now to paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 15 begins with the language: "Finally, through my contacts in the SDB, I was able to follow Milosevic's reaction to proposals for settling the crisis in Kosovo." Who are the contacts, plural, that you are referring to there?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same ones that I mentioned above, in both closed and open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You only mentioned one person, I think, in closed session yesterday -- two, two persons in closed session yesterday. You used the plural "contacts" here. Would that be those two persons?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean four different persons. Two were mentioned in paragraph 5, and the other two were mentioned in closed session. You mean "mnozina," right? They had their own contacts. So there's a multiplicity of things like these going on within the intelligence community. So the number you end up with is normally higher. It's not "mrdjina." I said "mnozina," which means plural. It says, "mrdjina."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that there were contacts you had in the SDB that you weren't going to reveal to us, and you gave us some reasons for that. And one of the reasons you gave us was that you knew they would simply wash their hands of you and say that you were lying, and that's one of the reasons you didn't want to give us the names. And, of course, that's -- can certainly be taken both ways. It could be that what they're going to do is tell the truth, and you're afraid of that and don't want us to find out their names. So as we go through this paragraph process and we get to a paragraph where there are people involved that you told us yesterday you didn't want to name, I want you to tell me that because I'm going to ask you for those names. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fail to understand your question. Mr. Mijatovic was mentioned. He was the chief of the Belgrade department of the State Security Service, which is the most powerful and biggest department in the whole of Serbia. He was the number two man virtually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, please, there are a number of questions which you appear not to understand, which I find it difficult myself -- where I find it difficult to understand your position. The questions -- the point that's being made is perfectly clear. You -- yesterday you refused on a number of occasions to name your source, and Mr. Ackerman just wants to be clear that when we are referring or you're referring in the statement or anything you say here to a source you're not prepared to name, you make that clear. And then he will follow it with a question, which will have to be dealt with when it arises. Just before moving on to that an expression I don't understand has been used in one of your answers and perhaps you can help me "mnozina," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a misinterpretation. It should have been the "plural, a couple of persons."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "Mnozina" is the word used by the witness in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it means "a couple" in the vernacular English, does it? We can move on now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Lied like to go to paragraph 40 now. In paragraph 40 you say this: "I was present at many meetings or receptions; for example, receptions on state occasions or JUL receptions, where I, because I had SDB approval, I was able to speak to Milosevic directly." Who did you get approval from, from SDB, that would enable you to speak to Milosevic directly? I don't understand how that works.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain to the Bench the technique that was used in Serbia, before I met with Milosevic. It goes for any meeting with any person. Whichever person is to attend a political meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If the Defence is interested in that, they will ask you to answer it. The questing is very simple: Who in the SDB gave you approval to speak to Milosevic directly? Just tell us that first.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who provided security vetting for my first meeting with Milosevic, and that needs to be checked in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you don't know who that was?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who signed in the archives, but I had a security - what word should I use in Serbian? - well, in any case, before anyone could approach Milosevic, he would ask the security service for information as to whether that person in terms of security is okay or not. Otherwise, you wouldn't be able to approach Milosevic; you couldn't brief him. And Mijatovic, a few months before I met Milosevic told me, "You'll go to see the boss." And I asked him, "How do you know?" And he said, "Well, it's standard procedure. He wanted to have intelligence data on you."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's good enough.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's good enough. I think you know the name of this person; why won't you tell us?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran Mijatovic told me that Mr. Milosevic asked information on me and on other participants. He said they ran their checks and that it was okayed and that I was going to see Milosevic. He told me that, but I don't know who signed it. Maybe it was another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... All right. You don't know. That's your position. I'm trying to get through this as painlessly as possible --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my answer. I apologise to the Bench. This is not my answer. "I don't know" was not my answer. I know clearly who told me that I was checked, that I was given the green light to see the president, and this was Zoran Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you say you don't know is who actually carried out the vetting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who signed it. It may have been Stanisic, Mijatovic, another civil servant. These are routine checks; however, Zoran Mijatovic was the person who told you me, You will go and see the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information was okayed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 48. It contains this language: "According to my sources in the SDB, initially Milosevic accepted this offer of assistance from the west to eliminate the UCK." "Sources in the SDB" as referred to here, just yes or no, are these persons you've already identified or not?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the persons I've identified publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you should read page 239 of that person's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I asked you for a yes or no. Please answer my question that way when you can. Paragraph 51: "I know through my SDB contacts that Milosevic also forbid the SDB to execute an international operation against Hashim Thaqi in Switzerland." Are these SDB contacts you've already identified to us or not, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 62, please. You talk about your knowledge of political agreements and so forth. You say: "I know about this from Tomic, Draskovic, Mihajlovic, and the SDB." The SDB information was provided to you by persons you've already identified to us or not, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before we move on that question, was there not an issue over privacy in relation to one of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. I think that first name is a different person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry, you're quite right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just yes or no, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 73, please. After halfway through this paragraph, you're referring to -- to your learning that Milosevic's position was the Albanian civilians were as guilty as the KLA. And you say: "Because" -- about some information. You say: "Because the SDB provided me with this information, they must have provided it to Milosevic." Now, the persons or person in the SDB that provided you with that information, are these persons you've already identified or not, just yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find the paragraph. 73?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a rather long paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is. About halfway down you'll find the language: "Because the SDB provided me with this information." You should be able to see the initials "SDB" fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The same publicly named persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're now going to paragraph 96. Halfway through paragraph 96: "I know through my SDB contacts that Milosevic did not authorise Stanisic to order SDB personnel in Kosovo to arrest the main Kosovo Albanian terrorists." The same SDB contacts you've already identified, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I wish to refer you to the material publicised by that person; namely, page 239 in that person's book. And I believe it was tendered by the Prosecution -- by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... About that person's book, Mr. Fila asked you a number of questions about the things he said about you and your trustworthiness and your character. And you said all those things were untrue, and yet you ask us to rely on his book when you say you were kidnapped as if all of a sudden he started telling the truth. Is his book untrue or true, and how would we know?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of it is true, part of it is half true, part of it is interpretation, as you could hear for yourselves. And it was not completely correct, as usual in intelligence work. Therefore, significant parts of that book are correct, some are incorrect, some are semi-correct. I don't know whether my answer suffices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it does. So your position is that half truths are usual in intelligence work?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One often has facts which, when tested, checked against several sources, amount to being 50 or 60 or 30 percent correct. You seldom encounter lies in intelligence work, but it is as seldom as a 100 percent correct information. Usually the percentage is between 60 to 90 percent, and it is a notorious fact for all intelligence agencies in the world. It is a complicated process. It involves different interpretations, perception. That's why you try to check against sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... And I take it that since you are yourself an intelligence operative, that we're getting quite a few half truths from you. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, that's an argument you may wish to advance in due course. For the moment, I think that will advance our knowledge of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 98, sir. "I know through my SDB contacts that Milosevic refused to officially support gathering information and evidence on UCK crimes against the Serbs." The SDB contacts mentioned there, are they persons you've already identified, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this involves another couple of people and some others I didn't mention. This is already 1999, and the initial two people were not in the service at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then one joined the service again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Tell us who the SDB contacts are that you're talking about in paragraph 98.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them are the same people. Two people who had publicly been named in 1999 were not with the service. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- see what kind of a trick you're trying to use here. The names were given in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I want you to give me the names of the people that are your SDB contacts that you referred to in 1998. This is not a trick. This is a legitimate question and the Judge will tell you so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm now confused. If you've already given us the names, either openly or in closed session, then the answer to the question would be that you've already identified them. But your initial answer indicated that there were two others not so far identified. And what you're being asked to do is identify them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, there seems to be a confusion. In 1999, there were two people whom I'd identified in closed session yesterday. The initial two persons I had named were not named in open session because at that time those two people were not with the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think I understand. Let's go then to paragraph 102. Near the beginning, second or third sentence: "In the beginning of 1998, based on my conversations with my SDB contacts," and then it goes on to talk about operations in Prekaz and the Jashari family and so forth. Who were the SDB contacts that you got that information from? If they are people you've already mentioned, just say that they are.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to paragraph 109. The first sentence: "Based on my conversation with members of the SDB and with Perisic, Milosevic ordered the army to give only minor resistance and not to engage NATO in serious battles." What members of the SDB gave you that information? Are they people you've already named? Answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In closed session -- I mean the people identified in closed session who conveyed that information from the top, as they explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I don't want to waste a bunch of time here. If your answer to the remaining paragraphs that I have to ask you about is going to be, "Yes, I've already identified them," contrary to what you told us yesterday, then I have no need to go through this exercise. Will that be your position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before -- don't answer that question. I don't think yet you have actually identified a passage of evidence in respect of which the witness yesterday refused to identify the source. So I think you do have to go through the exercise until we get to one which coincides with the various ones Mr. Fila put where there was a refusal to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in agreement with Mr. Fila, I didn't refer to any of the ones that had anything to do with Mr. Sainovic, and I won't today either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that. But it follows from that that there could be one there where the same issue arises. I don't think it's fair to the witness to say, "Is your answer going to be the same to every one I ask you about?" That would be taxing his memory I think beyond reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine. I'm sorry, I'm struggling to try to finish this cross-examination today, as you would like us to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, that was the message conveyed. But I also indicated to you if it has to go into tomorrow, it has to. And I'm very grateful for the efforts that are being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 110: "According to my conversations with SDB members, under Milosevic's orders, the army's main strategy was to hide from NATO attacks." Are these SDB members persons you have already identified, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in closed session. And I've explained the chain of information through which they received that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Let's go to paragraph 113, second sentence: "From my sources in the SDB, I learned that approximately the first week in June 1999, Milosevic ordered troops into the Djakovica region near the Albanian border." The sources in the SDB that you learned that from, have those been identified to us already or not, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one in closed session. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 118: "I know from my SDB contacts that the SDB provided Milosevic with maximum information about future targets," that's talking about NATO targets. The SDB contacts mentioned there, have they already been identified to us in open or closed session? Answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe we need to have a redaction at line 7, because that may identify the person who's been named in closed session based on the description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, since I don't think it's going to cause any great difficulty for anyone trying to follow the evidence, and it would be for the avoidance of any doubt or difficulty, I agree. And we will redact from the word "that's" to "there" in lines 7 and 8 on page 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question about paragraph 118 yet, I don't think. And what is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons identified in closed session, together with their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to paragraph 121. "During the bombing, I was authorised by the SDB and Milosevic to use my foreign contacts to contribute to finding an honourable way to stop the bombing." Who in the SDB authorised you? Is that someone whose name you've already given us; if so, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These people were the superiors of those people mentioned in closed session. The persons named in closed session couldn't issue such authorisation, but their superiors did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you've given us the names of their superiors, have you, that authorised this?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you do that, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aforementioned person, the person mentioned in closed session would be able to tell you who was up the chain of command, if he wishes to. I have knowledge about that but then it may be incorrect, since it was wartime and I cannot rely fully on my memory. And there was no time for us to sit down and discuss that. We had only very brief meetings and instructions issued. In any case, the authorisation came from the top via the person who was identified yesterday in closed session. Otherwise, I wouldn't have been able to leave the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the essence of that big long speech was you didn't know who it was. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the essence. I cannot give you an answer of which I can be certain. I can suppose and can speculate, but that's not my duty here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... And I don't want a guess. If you don't know, you don't know. Now I want to go to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I didn't know. I said I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you think you know, then tell us. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were superiors of the security service at the time. I can try and guess whether he was the person X or Y, but I cannot corroborate that. In any case, they were superior personnel; otherwise, it wouldn't have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot leave the country and be given communications equipment and money at wartime. You are being taken across the border, given corrode. You cannot do that without an approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... You've got me very confused. Because when I say your answer was you don't know who it was, you quarrel with that and tell us that's not true. Then when I ask you to tell us who it was, you say I would have to guess. Now, that makes no sense, Mr. Tanic. Why don't you pick one of those, and tell us which one is true. Do you know, or would you have to guess?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Finally, you posed the right question. Yes. I would have to guess. Because at the very top of the SDB, there were two or three people at the time. That's why I wouldn't like to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, why don't you just give us the two or three names, and we can ask all three of them, then.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The superiors of the SDB, at the time, it was Rade Markovic, Curcic, Radonjic [Realtime transcript read in error "Markovic"], Suvakovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Sudakovic"] was there as well. Take your pick. I would have to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on now to paragraph 125. You're talking about an agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, the transcript again 62, 4, the witness said Radonjic, not Markovic. No, no, he said Rade Markovic, Curcic, Radonjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. That's certainly consistent with my recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And not Sudakovic but Suvakovic. He was the ideologue; he wasn't an operative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're talking in 125 about the unilateral Easter cease-fire issue, which you say you found out through the SDB that Milosevic told Draskovic of this agreement. Who in the SDB provided you with this information? If it's someone you identified, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person was identified in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 129, please. You refer to some information there regarding General Pavkovic, and you say: "I know this partly from Vasiljevic and partly from the SDB." Who from the SDB did you learn this information? If it's someone you've already named, just say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 130, please. You're talking about your knowledge that Milosevic was prepared to wait until the last possible second before NATO troops entered Serbia. You say: "I have knowledge of this through the SDB." Who in the SDB? If it's someone you've already named, just say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The message was conveyed from the top. I don't know who gave that information at the top, but I got that from the person who was within the operative chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 131, please. "I know through my sources in the SDB that even after the war ended, Milosevic attempted to provoke war between NATO and Russia." Who in the SDB gave you that information? If it's someone you already named, just say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the superiors I mentioned were only to -- were given only to assist you. But as to who actually conveyed the messages, well you'll have to ask that to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your answer was yes, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer stands as it is recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript of the last answer doesn't look right. You say that,"The superiors I mentioned were only given to assist you. But as to who actually," and it's translated as, "conveyed the messages, you'll have to ask that to someone else." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You will have to ask the person identified in closed session, who conveyed the message. Whether it came from one of the three people at the top or from a fourth or a fifth person, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand now. I understand now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 143: "I know through my SDB and military contacts that both the army and the SDB have bad relations with the Republic of Serbia police." Who in the SDB provided you with that information? If it's someone you've already named, just say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons named in public session. It's a long story, been going on for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 151: "I know through my SDB contacts that Frenki Simatovic is the head of operational units, the so-called Red Berets." What SDB contacts provided you with this information? If you've already named them, just say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The person named in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 153: "According to my sources in the SDB and some individuals who are acquainted with both Arkan and myself, Milosevic had trouble engaging paramilitary forces in Kosovo." Sources in the SDB, are these persons you've already identified to us? If so, just say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons named both in closed and in open session, all four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 154: "I know through my SDB contacts and Perisic that Milosevic recruited ad hoc irregular special units to conduct operations in Kosovo." The SDB contacts referred to there are people who -- are they people who have already been identified to us? If so, just say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were identified both in the open and closed session, all of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 157: "According to some experts within ND, who have connections in the Ministry of Justice, and my sources in the SDB, Milosevic arrested 150 to 200 paramilitaries in Kosovo." The sources in the SDB, are these people you already identified to us? And if so, simply say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were named in both open and private session. I am always providing this explanation who was named in close session, who was name in open session, and we are referring to persons who are named in both private and open session. I say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 159, please, talks about the reporting of the numbers of casualties, what was in the newspapers, and what was suppressed. You say: "I received these estimates from the SDB and the military." Who in the SDB provided you with these estimates? If it's someone you've already named, just say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mentioned in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assessment of his --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 167, please: "I know through my former SDB contacts," referring to Mira Markovic,"that he is currently involved in directing SDB activities on a daily basis." The former SDB contacts you're referring to, are these persons you've already named for us in closed or open session? If so, just say "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this in the transcript at all. It says through my contacts. It doesn't say "former."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there's apparently a difference between the English and the B/C/S transcript in that regard. Forget about the word "former." The SDB contacts you're referring to there, are these persons you've already identified to us in closed or open session?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And finally paragraph 170, you talk about the SDB's evaluation of Pavkovic. Who in the SDB gave you this information? Is it somebody you've already named in either closed or open session?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person named in public session who wrote the book we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who conveyed the prevailing opinion, the opinion of the other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've gone through 30 instances, I believe, which are nearly all the mentions you made in your statement about SDB contacts. In page 22 of your testimony, the first day you testified here on direct examination, you named some persons with whom you'd had contact with the SDB. And you said:"But also a lot of other individuals who I would meet in the course of the number of years." And you haven't identified for us today a lot of other individuals. In fact, you haven't identified one other individual. So what did you mean when you said, "but also a lot of other individuals"?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see the entire sentence described to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no way of showing it to you. Let me see if I can do a little better; I probably can.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you read it -- the entire sentence out or maybe give me the context because I did meet many people, you know. I didn't work with all of them. Is there a full stop, comma, what is the context? Does it presume numerous other individuals from the service or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We got the message, Mr. Tanic, and we're looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, just -- I don't know. Maybe Mr. Hannis can help me with this a little bit. I want to read out to the witness the first 14 lines on page 22 of the first day's transcript, the 10 November transcript. This is the rough version, and this particular testimony was taken in closed session. But the part I want to read out doesn't reveal anything that -- I think doesn't relieve anything that can't be public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're looking, but the transcript I have has the consecutive numbers of 6200 and something, rather than page 22 for that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They don't always run consistently. We're looking. If Mr. Ackerman can indicate to me the subject maybe close or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's page 6277.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 6277, line 2 I think is where it starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bear in mind that part of that's in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It all is, Your Honour. It's actually 62 -- starts at 6276 on line 24, and that's the part that I would like to put to the witness down to the end of the -- of private session. I just want to make sure that I don't do that inappropriately. And I'd like Mr. Hannis to perhaps assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me read it to the witness. You named your primary contact, and this is in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in private or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- no, we're in open session, but listen to my question. You named your primary contact and that name was given in private session, so we will not use the name. You then said -- well, you indicated he -- but the question was: "You indicated he was your primary contact. Elsewhere in your statement, you refer to your sources at the SDB. When you used that term 'elsewhere in your statement,' what individuals were you referring to?" And you then go on to say: "Well, above all to these two individuals I have in mind," and you give the name, one is Mijatovic, and the other is the name is private session, "but also to a lot of other individuals I would meet in the course of the number of years. I have even forgotten some of their names now." Now, that's the passage that Mr. Ackerman is interested in and he wants to know why you've named so few individuals when you were referring to a lot of other individuals who you would meet in the course of the number of years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is very easy to explain. I got in contact with people for one day or half a day. Somebody would drive me somewhere, provide security, does a short operative task, then you exchange opinions,. And you hear for the fifth time something that you had heard from somebody else. In that context, I -- this is what I meant. Of course in operational matters, you get in contact with people that -- whose names you very soon forget or they do not use their real names. They would approach you and say, My name is that and that. They bring you a passport, drive you to the border. You sit down, light a cigarette, have a coffee, cup of coffee, and you hear from that person what you'd heard from five other people. These are operatives not of the lowest rank and many of them do not use their real name. They do not introduce themselves at all sometimes. So you can't expect all of them to say, Hello, I'm Markovic, et cetera. And even those whose names I do remember, I wouldn't want to entangle them in this. I've helped this Tribunal quite a lot by naming the people from the top. And this has opened and raised a very controversial issue for me and I've taken that risk on my shoulders and I believe named more people than I should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you just said something that really drew my attention. You talked about -- you said this: "I've helped this Tribunal a lot by naming the people from the top." And then you say this: "This has opened and raised a very controversial issue for me." How do you know? Have you been talking to people outside of this court about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not. But I know what it means to broach the intelligence dimension of political problems. This is tantamount to opening Pandora's box. And the two names I mentioned today, I mentioned in the Milosevic trial four years ago, and this means I probably have discussed this with somebody. Broaching the intelligence dimension means quite a problem for the witness, broaches a series of issues, and means that the witness has to bear quite a large burden. It's very complicated subject matter connected with very specific areas of life that may be subject by -- to abuse by the Defence, may be subject to a misunderstanding on the part of the public. So to broach an intelligence dimension of a political problem such as Kosovo is tantamount to a very large burden on me. I was less than willing to do so, but I did in the interest of justice to get to the truth. And, Mr. Ackerman knows quite well what kind of burden I undertook by doing so, and now you are being -- you are forcing me to name more names. Since from 1994 and 2001, I've got into contact with at least 30 to 50 members of that service. Somebody drove me to the border. Some beat me up. Some lauded me, and some beat up my wife. This is a very complex and -- relations with SDB of Serbia ranging from love to open disagreement. And now you're trying to exploit this dimension. I've never discussed this with anybody. I'm perfectly aware of being steeped in that job for 25 years at various levels. I'm a politician. Apart from that, I have a master's degree in politics. I know what it means to introduce an intelligence dimension into a political problem, such as Kosovo is. And this is opening a Pandora's box both for the witness and the Defence. And it is not that for the Defence because you may manipulate at will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... You've said all that. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, we're going elsewhere now. We got through the process. In being fair with you, because you're always accusing us, Defence counsel, of abusing you in some way - maybe you abuse us by doing that. But in any event, I want you to know that my thesis regarding your testimony is that you just make up answers which you think will sound good at the time. And I'm going to demonstrate that in the questions I'm getting ready to ask you. Now, yesterday during your testimony - and I'm at pages 23 and 24 starting I believe at line 19 on page 23 - you were answering a question and Judge Bonomy said to you: "Mr. Tanic, please get real. You are being asked for your recollection of events. You're not being asked for other people's recollections. You're not being asked to name any other individuals who were present on this occasion at this stage. You are simply being asked to explain accurately what happened. And you're persisting in refusing to address the apparent contradictions in the various explanations you've given. That leaves the Court -- remember, we're not politicians, we're not newspapers, we're not gossips in the street. We are a Court and Courts operate on facts. And if you won't assist us by giving the facts, then we will not be able to do justice." Mr. O'Sullivan then started to ask you another question and you interrupted and you said this: "Your Honours, may -- it is now clear my position. Can I try to help the Court finally to resolve this contradiction?" And you're talking about the conversation with Milosevic. "There was a conversation over the telephone and tete-a-tete, both occurred." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't understand why you're asking me this. I've already explained to the Court that, yes, of course when describing circumstances there are in my testimony things which may sound contradictory because there were so many events, and my memory doesn't serve me perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... And I'm going to explain --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- and you're going to find out why I'm asking that question right now. So just be patient. What was happening there was you were being challenged on a statement that you had had with Milosevic, when all you had done was overhear a telephone conversation. And you explained that to the Court with this answer, saying: "Both telephone and a tete-a-tete conversation with Milosevic." That's what you said. Now, I want to refer you to your testimony in Milosevic in that case, and that's where Milosevic was talking to you about whether or not you'd had any personal meetings with him. And you said: "Do you mean eye to eye, a tete-a-tete, just you and me" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I have a page reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try and find it. I'm having a little problem here with that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm content you ask the question as long as the reference is going to be found in due course within this session. So please go on with the question while someone else finds the particular reference for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If nothing else, I'll find it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me start over. Milosevic says this: "As far as I'm able to interpret this, you never had a personal meeting with me, did you?" And you said: "You mean eye to eye, a tete-a-tete, just you and me?" And then he said: "Any meeting." And then you said: "I'm waiting for the interpretation. Each of these times there was a meeting you and meet, never a tete-a-tete. There was always other people present. It was always a group of some kind." So when I say you made up answers just because you think they are going to sound good, that's what you did yesterday when you told Judge Bonomy that it wasn't just a telephone conversation, but a tete-a-tete meeting between you and Milosevic. You just made that up, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question there? So this is a lengthy tirade which accuses me of being a liar. Of course, you are bound to do that because you don't want to admit that because I'm in the right. Can you specify your question from all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm surprised that you don't understand the question, Mr. Tanic. But the question is inviting you to explain the apparent inconsistency between telling Milosevic that you never had a tete-a-tete with him and telling us yesterday that you did. And what we would like to know is the explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? If there are several people somewhere and then you take a couple of steps with the president aside, could you describe this as an eye to eye or a meeting with other people present? There were occasions when other people attended. And you know you take somebody to the side or you are taken to one side for five, seven, ten minutes, this is a tete-a-tete meeting, but in a -- in the context of other people being present. And nobody else would know what transpired between us. And you cannot name all of these people because some meetings were controversial, secret, and some people would deny having attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And apart from that. Sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a perfectly understandable explanation. Can you then explain your answer in Milosevic, which was each of these times there was a meeting you and me, never a tete-a-tete, there was always a group present of some kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is why I've asked for the page reference, because I think there was a somewhat similar explanation about that answer in Milosevic as he's just given related to the answer and I need to find the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 5016, 19 through 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you'll be able to deal with it, Mr. Hannis, in due course. But bearing that explanation you've just given in mind, can you explain the answer you gave in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? I could not provide any explanation for my answer to Milosevic for the simple reason that you may follow what kind of proceedings that was. It was an argument between the two of us, and that was all it was. And finally, I gave up from testifying against Milosevic - and this is perfectly clear from the transcript - he negated everything. He denied that he ever set eyes on me, that we ever worked together. He denied everything; and in such a situation I just said, Okay, I will stick to verifiable things and this is what I said. And I did not mention the things that could not be verified. And this trial is much more regular. Milosevic really attacked me as a beast, if you monitored that trial, and at this trial I can collect my thoughts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I know in the Milosevic case that before you testified you swore to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And I know in this case before you testified you swore to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Now, when you say in Milosevic you never had a tete-a-tete meeting with him, and when you say in this case that you did have a tete-a-tete meeting with him, one of those is not true. And telling things that are not true, under oath, is an offence in this Tribunal called perjury, are you aware of that, for which you can receive a pretty serious sentence and fine?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am aware of that. But simply in the Milosevic trial, I simply told the Court that given the circumstances obtaining, I will testify to facts that could be proven or verified. There were people at our meetings. If you do not say everything, this is not lying. You simply did not say everything. I would have then been testifying for 20 days if I were to tell everything. In that case, I chose examples which could be verified to avoid further argument. If you omit saying something which happened, doesn't mean that you are lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you didn't omit anything. You said exactly what you said. And now are you saying to us that you lied in Milosevic just because you gave up and he was treating you like a beast? Is that what you're saying? Because let me tell you, it's perjury either way.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, it is stated in the transcript that I informed the Bench that I would be testifying to things that can be verified by two or three sources. The Bench was not happy with that, but that was my testimony at that point in time. I thought it would be in the best interests of the justice and the Court, and subsequently I was borne out by certain developments. Now I can testify about many more events because in the meantime events borne out my testimony in the Milosevic trial. And they were not known to be correct at the time of the Milosevic trial. In the meantime, they've been verified as true, and now I can testify in a much more relaxed atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've used this button I have here to cut off a witness here for the first time in this trial because I'm not satisfied you're trying to answer the question. No Court will tolerate a witness coming in and answering only questions he chooses to answer. And the Milosevic Tribunal certainly did not tolerate that as an approach that was acceptable. So going down a side-road into a discussion of that is simply a smoke-screen to avoid answering the question. You're being asked to explain why you said in Milosevic that you did not have a tete-a-tete meeting with him at any stage, and we would like a straightforward answer to that question. Can you give us it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, first of all, because I was under a great deal of emotional strain and stress; secondly, because I had been subjected to extreme propaganda from Belgrade during his trial, things that I was shown; and thirdly, because there was no way for me to prove that. The principal reason being the emotional strain and the extreme propaganda launched against me that was shown me during the actual trial. I was sadly affected by the fact that my party seemed to have washed their hands of me as well as some of my friends. They could have said things like, "All right, we don't agree with you testifying. We don't approve of it," that sort of thing. But what they did really affected me in a very sad way. My emotional state during my testimony in the Milosevic case was a complex one, must have been a slip of the tongue during that particular altercation and what I eventually said must have been a result of my condition at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Tanic, I think you've probably been pretty successful in your life dancing around the truth and getting away with it. I assure you you're not going to get away with it in this court. And I suggest to you that what you told us yesterday is your attitude about whether or not you need to be truthful in this court. Page 20 of yesterday's transcript Judge Bonomy stopped you and said: "Are you now refusing to answer the question? It's not for you to decide whether you'll answer on matters that can be corroborated. It's your job to answer every question that's put to you. Now I ask you, please answer the question." And then you said this: "But what was the question? Whether I had two meetings with him," meaning Milosevic, "one conversation with him, direct conversation," meaning Milosevic. And then you said this: "I can say whatever I wish because that man is no longer alive, so he can't challenge anything I say so I'll just make stuff up." That's what you were saying, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I really must say. I didn't understand. I still fail to understand why I'm being asked questions about Milosevic. He's no longer alive; case closed. I just said this to show that my intentions were honourable and that I did not intend to be telling the Court all kinds of things. It's a simple misunderstanding, truly. This man died. And this is not a subject on the agenda of this trial as far as I understand, which is the reason I fail to understand the original question. I can say all sorts of things, well, yes. But that is not what I was doing. I tried to stick to the very substance. When it comes to substance, I try to be very consistent, that's at least my impression. It is true that some of the circumstances are quite confusing. My personal destiny is a sad one. It has been and still is. Every time I give evidence this presents an emotional problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's stop dancing and start dealing with the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I certainly consider there's a context to that particular answer that you've identified which relates to the question of giving evidence only about things that can be corroborated. I think it's only right to take it in its proper context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly one context it could be in, Your Honour, but it could be otherwise also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to move to another matter. I'm going to go to paragraph 4 of your statement now. In paragraph 4 of your statement you tell us this: "I was chosen to conduct discreet negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians. I received this authorisation directly from Milosevic in a meeting that I and Dusan Mihajlovic held with him in approximately 1995." Now, it wouldn't be a mistake for one reading that to get the impression that there was a private meeting between you and Milosevic and Mihajlovic where he said, "Ratomir Tanic, because of all your training and skill and wonderful contacts, I'm choosing you to conduct discreet negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians." That would be a logical conclusion one could draw from reading that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but that's not the conclusion. You will say again that I'm dancing the truth. First of all, Milosevic said I had good contacts with the Kosovo Albanians. He asked for me to be vetted, as I explained before. He knew this from before and so did Dusan Mihajlovic. You simply can't understand that Mr. Milosevic told me, "There you are, Mr. Tanic, you have wonderful contacts. Here's your authorisation." He was the president after all. I was very specific when I described that scene. It wasn't a private meeting. It was an official meeting between the delegation of our party, Milosevic, and two of his associates, if I remember correctly, who were -- that were sometimes there. Dusan Mihajlovic and I were the only two people doing the briefing; that's why I mentioned those two names. We put this plan to him. Milosevic said, "This is fine. You can go ahead with that." That's what authorisation means in purely political terms. He certainly didn't tell me what his opinion of me was. If that opinion had been a poor one, he probably wouldn't have come to that meeting to begin with. He would have said, "I don't want to see that person." Had he not known I had good contact with the Albanians and I had worked on that he probably would have said, "Oh, god, where did you get this idea." I don't think Milosevic would have enlisted my assistance. If you start twisting my words like that and quoting them out of context, the impression can be a grotesque one. You're telling me that I'm dancing a dance around the truth. I apologise to the Court every time I was wrong when I said something. My situation is a very difficult one while giving evidence and what you're trying to do is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your position that if I quote from your statement I'm twisting your words, or is that your twist that's in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in that last question, he didn't quote from his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He referred to it as a private meeting and he flowered it up with all kinds of terms of why he was selected. That's not in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "I was chosen to conduct discreet negotiations" -- I read it absolutely word for word, Your Honour. I'm prepared to go to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I don't see anything inappropriate in how that was presented. The statement was quoted and then a gloss was put on it as an impression that can be gleaned from it, and the witness was asked to say if that is fair or not. And instead of dealing directly with it and giving us the exact circumstances in which there was a delegation of more than the two of them from the one side and Milosevic had two with him, instead of giving us that straightforward explanation which it would be pretty simple to give, we go into a suggestion that this is somehow or other misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess my objection is, Your Honour, when he phrases it: Would it be from that quote that I just gave you unfair to assume the following? Well, it would be possible to assume a thousand things from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it might be, Mr. Hannis, but it's perfectly reasonable to assume that there were only three of them at the meeting, and it's equally appropriate for the witness then to explain that that was not the case. If we could nail the facts in that simple way, we would make far better progress towards justice in this case. It's time for another break and that may be merciful. We must go into closed session while Mr. Tanic leaves the court, and we'll remain that way until he returns.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, do you remember testifying in the Milosevic case that you only met with Mr. Milosevic either five or seven times -- five to seven times?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I meant was the important meetings, the ones where relevant issues were discussed; that was the context. I did meet him many times, as I said at the time, but some of the meetings were simply irrelevant. I said exactly how many times I met certain persons just to tell you about the pace of our political life, and I think I was pretty specific at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I want to go to paragraph 6 of your statement now. "In my capacity as negotiator, on several occasions I presented my work to Milosevic directly. I met with Milosevic directly in relation to Kosovo and international issues approximately six to ten times." Now, the truth is what we learned earlier today, and that is that you never had a tete-a-tete meeting with Mr. Milosevic, but you were always in some kind of a group, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what people might take this to mean. If we're together with other people and we go to one side, is that something you define as a tete-a-tete meeting, or is that a meeting within a group? Someone might call that a tete-a-tete. We're talking about something that no one else can hear. Someone else might tell you this is a meeting within a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... We don't need to have it again, and I understand what you're saying. You talk in that paragraph I just read to you, you used the words "in my capacity as a negotiator," right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of the negotiators. I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just curious --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On first that day --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's good enough. I am just curious about something. In the Milosevic case - I'm on page 5104 - Judge Robinson intercedes and asks you this: "Mr. Tanic, what you're saying is that you were one of the driving forces in the negotiations, not the principle negotiator." And then you said to Judge Robinson this: "That's right. From a formal and legal point of view, I was not a negotiator." So is that the case? You really weren't a negotiator in legal and formal terms?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That should have read: "I was not the main negotiator." In a formal sense, I was not the chief negotiator. But I was the driving force behind the negotiations, and I think my evidence was consistent at the previous trial and the present one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your response to that is that that's a mistake in the transcript, that you didn't say that? Is that what you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. You should go back to the audio-tape. There was an altercation and perhaps there wasn't time for me to interject and say I wasn't the chief negotiator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The final question I want to ask you about that is: What are the legal and formal terms that one would use to describe a negotiator, since you say that you were not the such in legal and formal terms? What formal and legal terms are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the president's decision. Under the law, as far as I know, he has the power to issue instructions and orders that are as good as a law. He, for example, comes up to Mr. Ratko Markovic and says,"You're the chief negotiator," then Ratko Markovic is the chief negotiator, which is what I've been saying. He was the chief negotiator in these discreet negotiations. I was never told my Milosevic that I was the chief negotiator. So that's what I had in mind. He was after all the president of Serbia, and it was down to him to say who was the chief negotiator or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right -- [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was as good as a law, his word, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would like to go to paragraph 11. In paragraph 11 you say this: "I am certain that members of the SDB, Milutinovic and Mihajlovic, presented my work on these negotiations to Milosevic and that Milosevic received reports on my progress on a daily basis." So you know, do you, that every day someone from SDB or Milutinovic or Mihajlovic went to Milosevic to report what you had accomplished that day, every day; true?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I was convinced, but I didn't say that it was like that. As far as the -- I was aware of the way Milosevic's government worked. He would always start every day with a briefing in the morning, a security briefing. That happened every day. Whether Stanisic briefed him directly every morning or sent a report to him in view of a briefing, I don't know. I don't suppose that he was briefed every day, but I know that Milosevic's day always began with a security briefing. After all, when we talked about a variety of issues, he told me that I was always to read these security reports every day that there were negotiations, but not every day when there were no negotiations in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you if he got a security briefing every day. I asked you if you are certain, like you say, that he was briefed on a daily basis about your work in the negotiations, because that's what you said. Now, do you really want to tell this Chamber that that's true, that every day somebody said to Milosevic, "Okay, here's what Tanic did today." Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were negotiations in progress that had already gone on for five or six days, then this would be a daily thing. When there were no negotiations in progress, he certainly wouldn't go around saying things such as, "Tanic did this or did that." So I place this clearly in the context of negotiations, when negotiations were in progress. That's what I'm saying. It wasn't the case every day, but when negotiations were in progress, he was briefed on a daily basis. Based on the information I received from Mr. Mijatovic, within an hour and an hour and a half, he would have a report on his table on everything that was going on, because that went directly through Stanisic's office and would normally reach Milosevic. If Mijatovic misinformed me, then I simply was told something that wasn't accurate. I didn't walk up to Milosevic to ask him if he had been receiving daily reports. But when negotiations were in reports, I am certain that reports were a daily thing because I didn't need to have feedback after all, did I? Later on, the whole thing was explained. There was an entire paragraph explaining the methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want you to explain something to us. This is in paragraph 38. Now, you were -- even though you've now backed off of it, you did say in some statements that you were the principal negotiator. You certainly contend that you were the most successful negotiator, and the driving force behind these negotiations. Paragraph 38 you say this in the middle of the paragraph: "At the end of 1997, I asked a couple of people what was going on with the negotiations." Now, if you're the driving force and the most successful negotiator and the main power behind this negotiation process, why on earth are you asking other people what's going on in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's talk here of implementation of the education agreement. I wasn't involved with that simply because this was implementation pure and simple, nothing more. Ratomir Vico was in charge of implementing that agreement, not Ratko Markovic. The negotiations had to do with confidence-building measures. Once a certain measure had been agreed, we'd move on to the next set of measures. And Milosevic would set up a special commission to deal with education-related issues. When I asked about those negotiations, those were the negotiations that I had in mind, the negotiations regarding the education system. I don't see any particular discrepancy there, which of course is for the Chamber to judge, but negotiations were about the entire process. Whenever we were successful in something, we would have that particular settlement implemented one way or another, and then we would just move on. We had massive amounts of issues that were tabled and negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 52, please. You're talking about one your conversations with Perisic, and this has been referred to more than once in your testimony. You say: Perisic stated that in February or March of 1998, the SDB and the VJ began cooperating and organised a state fact-finding mission to Kosovo. The purpose of this fact-finding mission was to get an accurate picture of what was happening in Kosovo, what was the extent of the threat of terrorism, and what measures to use with the threat." The first question I want to ask you about is: In February and March of 1998, what position did Perisic hold?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the chief of the General Staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Microphone. Come on, mike man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your position that the Chief of the General Staff, in February and March of 1998, didn't know what was going on in Kosovo; and thus had to send a fact-finding mission there to find out what was going on? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That doesn't follow from this paragraph. Please. The context is altogether different. I explained, didn't I, that Perisic and Stanisic had started working together. They joined forces, and along with a number of other politicians, tried to change Milosevic's mind. You have Stanisic's evidence about that and you have Perisic's evidence about that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a question. I don't think you understood my question because it doesn't sound like you're answering it. My question was: Is it really your position that the Chief of the General Staff didn't know what was going on in Kosovo; and thus had to send a fact-finding mission, be part of one, down there to find out what was happening? Now, is that your position? And if you will answer that question, yes or no, then maybe we can go on. I don't need a further explanation right now.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't entirely certain, at least that's what he told me. I told you about the conversations with Perisic. He said that he did not have that kind of perspective in terms of intelligence. There were problems as to who would be controlling the border, who would be providing the equipment for electronic surveillance of the border. He wanted to have the intelligence perspective. He had the military perspective, his own perspective, but he needed to have an intelligence in on this situation. This was a synergy of efforts. Everyone has their own perspective. I have a political perspective and not a military perspective, and the same thing applies to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So, now you have answered that. Now, I want to ask you something else about that. You're talking about this fact-finding mission, where there was this helicopter flight that you claim Perisic told you about, right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If what he said wasn't true, then I was misinformed. All of my information relating to General Perisic stems from what he said, or rather, from our conversation back in 1999. I hadn't known Mr. Perisic previously, and I did not interfere with military issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In addition, it's your position that your information from Operation Horseshoe came from General Perisic, your information about this helicopter flight. Those are two pieces of information that he was the source for; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was crystal clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to make sure we were all on the next page before I ask you the next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that there was a question in line 10 in which you're quoting as saying, "I have a military perspective and not the political one, and the same thing applies to him," and I suspect you said the opposite of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I have a political perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's just to clarify it. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you testified in Milosevic, General Perisic was interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor for eight days; the 6th, the 7th, and the 8th of December, 2003, and the 23, 24, 25, 26, and 27 of January, 2004. Now, would it surprise you to know that General Perisic never mentioned your name, never mentioned the helicopter incident, and never mentioned Operation Horseshoe?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that would greatly surprise me. In that case, you should call General Perisic, since our conversations did take place. And I think they were even recorded, because I think there must have been some eavesdropping going on in Perisic's house at the time. The house must have been bugged. I can't be certain about that, but I think you should call General Perisic. I would be comfortable confronting him or anyone else to contradict my statement. There's no problem at all about that. I have no vested interest in lying to anyone or deluding anyone. My position is what it is. Very often you get people saying one thing in a court of law, writing something else in their books, and saying yet a third thing privately. I heard at least four kinds of information about myself; one in court, another thing in the book, and a yet third thing was said in the newspapers. People say things about me that were out of what I testified to in court, 95 percent was true. They send a book to the Court and yet they claim not to know me. I can hardly be expected to know about everything going on. As far as I know, Mr. Perisic confirmed that he knew he at a trial in The Hague and also in a newspaper interview. You can go and ask him again perhaps because, to say the least, I would be somewhat surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've had an awful long answer to a very simple question. Again, please restrict your answers to what's necessary to answer the question, Mr. Tanic. Mr. Ackerman, are you privy to the questions that were asked in the course of the interview, or do you simply have a record of what answers were given?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the entire transcripts of those interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were questions asked about his knowledge of the helicopter incident or the name Tanic or Operation Horseshoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would have to conduct an additional search of the transcript before I would be comfortable in my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am told that there was specific question about there being some kind of a plan which could have triggered, I suppose, the horseshoe issue. He never spoke about horseshoe, and I believe he said there wasn't any plan that he knew of either. But I don't want to be quoted with regard to that without consulting it further, Your Honour, and doing a more further search into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I only tried to find out if Mr. Tanic's name was mentioned, if the horseshoe issue were mentioned, and if the helicopter incident were mentioned; and none of them were I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At paragraph 67, Mr. Tanic, the issue you're talking about there is whether a foreign military presence would be allowed in Kosovo ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The issue was whether a foreign military presence would be allowed in Kosovo.
