And what you said there was: "I had discussions on this matter with ambassadors and diplomats of the EU countries." First, give me the names of the ambassadors that you had discussions with about foreign military presence in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The British ambassador, I think his name was Donald; and the Italian ambassador, Baskoni, Francesko Baskoni; after that there was Ricardo Sosa; the Hungarian ambassador, whose name escapes me right now; the German ambassador, Mr. Gruber; an American envoy; and their closest associates, the embassy's sector, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a name been recorded as Donald, but you've previously referred to this name as Donnelly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Donnelly. I think his name is Robert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how about the American envoy, what's that name?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The charge d'affaire, I forget who it was at the time. The name escapes me. They didn't have an envoy, but they didn't have an ambassador either, so it was a charge d'affaire who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you talk about having conversations about this with diplomats of the EU countries. Can you give me the names of any these diplomats who you had these discussions with.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are at the same time diplomats of the EU, their closest associates. I would have to check my notes for secretaries of embassies, but these are EU member country diplomats. Ambassadors are diplomats of those countries. We discussed with the European Union itself about these matters. I believe that at the time Mr. Stefano Sannino was one of the diplomats of the European Union itself, with whom we discussed these matters. But really, I would have to go through my archives. Many people were involved. I believe I've named enough of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have notes and archives, do you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have anything, Mr. Ackerman. You know that very well. We had books and everything else stolen from us. I don't have any documents, no photo archives. My political party does not want to access to them, and this is why at times it is very difficult for me during testimony to remember certain things. All documents, all books have been stolen from us, and this is verifiable. And now I can produce to the Court a list of cover letters or invitations for certain meetings. It accidentally was left in one of my photo albums and one photograph with Milosevic, but it was -- it is now currently in the country that I'm residing in. I haven't brought them with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember a little earlier when we talked about dancing around the truth. And your answer starting at line 7 just now, page 93, you said: "I'd have to check my notes." And then a little further down you said: "I'd have to go through my archives." And then I say: "Oh, you have notes and archives, do you?" And you say: "No, I don't have anything." Now, that just doesn't wash. That's you dancing around the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not dancing about the truth. There is a notebook, and this is everything that I kept, Mr. Ackerman. The Court may verify how many meetings I held. These are material facts. The core diplomatic in Belgrade knew me. And we had, through Mr. Sannino we had access to certain -- please, what do you want me to say that I never anybody? And do you want me to claim like Milosevic did that I never lived? This is why this is an emotional issue for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please hold on, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Tanic, do you still have a notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one small notebook. Because I took it with me to Hungary when I fled the country, and it is now kept in the country where I live in right now. There are telephone numbers and notes. But when it comes to archives, my party has the archives and the notes, and they can be consulted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you said: "I'd have to check my notes," and "I'd have to go through my archives," you're referring to one little notebook that you had in the archives of your party, and you really weren't trying to mislead this Chamber. Is that your position now?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I want to verify some telephone numbers of some people in the US or names, if it's necessary for the purpose of this trial. It's a small notebook. Only -- the only document that may refresh some names in my memory, but I had many meetings with diplomats in Belgrade where we discussed these issues. And these are EU diplomats because the countries named are member countries. And sometimes I meant the Russians --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Stop. You don't want to answer my question and I understand that, so you can stop. And I'll ask you something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, don't assume that I for one from drawn from you the same inference as you seek to draw from the answers given, Mr. Ackerman. You have to take all that's been said by the witness together, before concluding what this is all about. The comments can be made in submissions in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, 67, of your statement, where you talk about meeting with all these ambassadors and diplomats; you used both terms, "ambassadors" and "diplomats," did these meetings all take place in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were some meetings abroad; and ambassadors at the same time diplomats really --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you say "I had discussions on this matter," you use the word "I," "I had discussions on this matter." Do you really mean to tell us that you had discussions face-to-face with these ambassadors and diplomats that you have named; with each one of them, you, face-to-face discussions? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course and with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. May I supplement my answer which is: Yes. I'm not changing it. Relatively, often I emphasise, I would have meetings with political directors at ministries of foreign affairs abroad. They were usually engaged with us. If I may, I can refresh my memory. Maybe I may invoke Mr. Martin Lutz. He was one of such people who was involved quite a great deal in this process, and I hope he has ample archive material. It would be more useful to us to call him, rather than to bother Mr. Talja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tanic. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Paglia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some meetings with other people that you have not mentioned in your statements and ask you if you actually -- whether or not you had meetings with any of these people or talked with them. Did you ever have any meetings or talk with President Clinton of the United States?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how about Prime Minister Blair of the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Madeleine Albright, the Secretary of State, heavily involved in the Kosovo matter, did you ever talk with her?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Richard Holbrooke of the United States, heavily involved in Kosovo negotiations, did you ever talk with him or negotiate with him?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not negotiate. I believe that once, very briefly, we exchanged opinions at a reception. But I spoke to all associates of the people you mentioned, close associates of Mr. Blair, Madeleine Albright --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Christopher Hill, how many meetings did you have with Christopher Hill? He was the principle negotiator for the United States with regard to Kosovo. Now, you, as a major negotiator for Yugoslavia, you must have met with Christopher Hill on many occasions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that misstates his evidence, and I object to the relevance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Misstates whose evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic's, Your Honour. He indicated he was involved in discreet negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians; not with the Americans about Kosovo, but with the Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he says over and over that he met with ambassadors and diplomats and envoys and all these people about Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In a set of negotiations, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. He said he was negotiating with representatives of all these various countries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was I ever -- was I ever -- did I ever say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, when this sort of thing happens, you remain silent until the thing is resolved. I see nothing wrong with the question. Continue, please, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't even insist on the word "negotiations." I just want to know how many meetings he had with the principal American negotiator regarding Kosovo, Mr. Christopher Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Christopher Hill was not chief negotiator for the Serbian Albanian political dialogue concerning Kosovo, neither did he meddle with it. His associate in the US embassy was included on an information reception level. He was the envoy for the problem of Kosovo on behalf of the US, Mr. Hill. And he was the envoy at the time when his brother also worked in the US embassy in Belgrade, with whom I would occasionally meet. And as far as Christopher Hill himself was concerned, he operated in the time when New Democracy and Milosevic took separate views with regard to Kosovo. And he was involved when our negotiations with Kosovo, together with international intermediaries, were side-tracked. I used to meet his brother on several occasions. He most probably knows what his brother was talking about with me, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Personal envoy regarding the KLA was Lawrence [sic] Gelbard. How many times did you meet with Lawrence Gelbard?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have a time-frame for these, because this witness has testified that he was involved in negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians from 1995 to 1997. Now, if these questions are regarding people who had positions in 1998 and 1999, then I object to the relevance of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he claims to have been meeting with various representatives, foreign governments, almost right up until the time he left Belgrade. So he talks about negotiations that he conducted and meetings that he had after the bombing started; and certainly before the bombing started, Mr. Gelbard and Mr. Hill were both very active in dealing with Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The relevant period is from 1995, Mr. Hannis, and therefore if -- the question will be read in that light. And the question is whether you met Mr. Gelbard, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke with him, but this could not be described as a meeting. Mihajlovic and I spoke to him briefly at a reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, because of your importance as the most successful and -- I can't remember your other word right now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's not ask provocative questions; let's try and encourage answers that help us by directing them to -- by directing us to the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A number of people have written books about this period of time in Serbia and Kosovo. Tim Judah wrote a book called "Kosovo: War and Revenge." Do you find it strange that you're not mentioned in that book?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that. The author who writes a book, whether he puts a person in or not, is not necessarily a reflection of what role this witness played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In other contexts I might have agreed with you, Mr. Hannis, but not on this one. I will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, without some foundation of what the particular focus of Mr. Judah's book is, I maintain this is irrelevant. If he's focusing on the combat, that's one thing; but we don't have a foundation for what Mr. Judah's focus was in his book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, are you familiar with this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it was published -- when it was published, this is an important piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're not familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is -- this book is not known to me. I know Tim Judah; I spoke to him on several occasions. This is why I'm asking you: When was this book published? Was it published --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter when it was published to establish whether or not you are familiar with it. Could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's not known to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think Mr. Hannis's second intervention does have some foundation in it, Mr. Ackerman. Can you elaborate a little on a basis for a foundation for the question that you ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Mr. Judah's book is an effort of him, as near as I can tell, to give a very comprehensive background of the conflict and the war itself, and the various efforts that were made to settle it, keep it from happening, things of that nature. And that's my recollection of the book that I read some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. But you see the answer the witness has given that he's not familiar with the book means that the question is pointless, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's not pointless. I don't think whether or not he appears in that book has anything to do with his familiarity with it, but with Mr. Judah's familiarity with him as this high-powered negotiator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, that's like saying to me there's a book written called "Little Women," are you surprised you're mentioned in it? My immediate reaction might be: Yes. But without having read it and knowing the whole subject matter, I couldn't give you a meaningful answer to the question. So as presently framed, I consider that this is not a question this witness could answer in a way that would be meaningful for us, so please move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] A better analogy might be if a book was written about outstanding jurist of Scotland in the 20th century, clearly, your name would be in it if there was such a book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, bearing in mind we're now in the 21st century, Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- there may be no surprise at all about that. So let's move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with General Clark's book, "Waging Modern War" about NATO and Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have any meetings with or discussions with General Clark?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely no. At that time I did not speak to him. Excuse me, when did I claim that I was chief negotiator, that I was very important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, just, please, again restrain yourself. I think we are reaching the point of diminishing returns, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll go elsewhere, Your Honour. I'm finished with that anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 77 you say this: "Perisic told me, in the conversation that I had with him while preparing my book, that he gave a written order in late spring 1998 to local commanders not to undertake any operations that were not signed by him." Now, a very simple question: Have you seen that order?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that I was told by him -- I did not say "showed to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I only want to know if you've seen the order. Now, you also claim that actions went on anyhow, in spite of this order. And you say this: "The military actions that took place anyway were undertaken on Milosevic's order through General Nebojsa Pavkovic, then the commander of the 3rd Army, now the VJ Chief of Staff." Now, these actions you talk about, these were actions that were taking place in the spring and summer of 1998, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it follows from the context of my talks with Perisic in its entirety. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All I'm trying to nail down with you right now is the date. The date when these -- when Perisic issued this order that you're talking about and when these actions went on, anyway, had to be spring and summer of 1998, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had issued this order at the end of spring, so it's summer 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- beginning of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know by the end of 1988, that General Perisic was no longer in the position of Chief of Staff of the army -- 1998, right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that from October or November ceased to be Chief of General Staff and not from summer. After the agreement with Holbrooke, he was displaced from that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so what you are claiming here, or at least what you claim Perisic told you, is that he issued this order in the spring of 1998; and that in spite of that in the spring and summer of 1998, Milosevic issued orders that went straight to General Pavkovic, who was commanding the 3rd Army at that point, bypassing General Perisic. That's what your claim is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the content of the information received from General Perisic, and it was complimentary to information that were relayed through intelligence channels. And the main source of that statement was General Perisic; I believe it's perfectly clear from the context. I never claimed anything. I relayed the content of our conversation, and you are claiming that I'm claiming something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think -- I take it you relayed that conversation as accurately as you possibly could. You didn't make any of that up, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And, as I said, it is complimentary to all other information received through intelligence channels. And in this context, I found that information to be trustful, because it was similar to what was reaching me from the top of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Okay. Let's take a look --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similar opinions --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at an exhibit and see about this. Let's look at Exhibit 4D35. Now, do you see that exhibit over there on the B/C/S version of it? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that says that Pavkovic was appointed 3rd Army commander in December of 1998, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to 4D36 now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says also that from the position of the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what it says. But let's look at 4D36 now. Now, I think if you look at this document you'll find that General Pavkovic didn't take up his duties as 3rd Army commander until 13 January of 1999; true?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the question that I have for you is when you say in paragraph 77 that Milosevic was issuing orders through Pavkovic, commander of the 3rd Army, in the spring and summer of 1998, are you the one that made that up or does that -- or did Perisic get that wrong?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean I invented that Mr. Pavkovic was replaced or moved, or that Perisic was not that -- he was commander of the Pristina Corps and then he was moved to the -- what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you know exactly what I mean. You say in your statement that Pavkovic was the commander of the 3rd Army in the spring and summer of 1998; and now you know that's wrong. Now, where did that come from? Did you make that up, or did Perisic tell you that? Now, that's a simple question; just answer it.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perisic did not say this, and neither did I invent that. It's just -- lacks precision. The Pristina Corps had to be inserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it lacks precision in a statement that you have sworn is the truth. Are we back to this is just a working document that you really don't adopt?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not going back to that. God forbid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he indicated when he adopted his statement that was true to the best of his information and belief. He's indicated in his early testimony today that he's a political guy not a military guy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these are all arguments to be weighed in due course. Mr. Ackerman, we're going to have to stop now. An outside observer might feel you've had a fair crack at the whip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Judge, it has gone a lot more slowly than I anticipated. I figured I'd be done well ahead of this, but we get very long answers. And I still have a significant amount to deal with. I'd say I've got another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we can allow that, I'm afraid, because there's got to be a starting point for controlling the length of cross-examination; otherwise, we're dealing with an endless trial. It cannot be that way. I've asked you all in the past to prioritise and that was working pretty well. And it has to work even with witnesses of the significance that you place on this witness. And I feel that the Chamber has plenty to go on so far as questions of general credibility and reliability are concerned, and that questions ought to be much more pointedly dealing with particular facts, as the last ones have been. But it may be that with that guidance you can tailor it to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly will undertake to do that, but I must say, for the record, that there's not been a witness that covers as much of the indictment as this witness. He covers paragraphs 17 through 69, paragraphs 77, paragraphs 79 to 101 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I say, Mr. Ackerman, I'm well aware of that. But I have to also take account of the evidence of witnesses yet to come, the significance that their evidence will have, that this may just be the first of many who -- for whom similar arguments could be advanced. And we do have to have some measure of control. So I'm asking you to look again at what has to be done in the remaining time. We also have another issue tomorrow that special interpretation arrangements will be in place for the next witness, and it's important to get started on him fairly early tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, and I'm telling you that I will do that. But you know that prior to this trial I tried very hard to get a severance because I knew this was going to happen to me. You let counsel for the other accused in this case so far cross-examine as long as they wanted to. Now when it comes to Mr. Pavkovic you're telling me that I can't cross-examine as long as I want to and I can't ask the questions that I think are necessary for his Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman, you know I haven't said that. And you know that to take the line that you're taking at the moment sounds like an attempt to establish a position in relation to possible future proceedings here. I will always allow questions that you can justify as necessary. But you know, as well as everyone else in the courtroom, that in a case of this nature we have to prioritise. There will be things which significant -- which though significant are of marginal significance. Now, with witnesses of this range, you and many others with experience and ability would be able to cross-examine for many, many hours. But in the real world, it's not possible. So I'm not stopping you raising issues of significance. I'm asking you to reflect on how much it is necessary for you to ask. As I said earlier today, if the cross-examination has to go on a bit longer, it has to go on a bit longer, but I'm relying on your professional experience to try to specify me to exercise adequate control over the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say one more thing just for the record if nothing else. I really do appreciate what you just said to me and I agree with that. But when you say to me that you'll allow questions if I can justify their necessity, I must reflect back to the first two accused who asked questions in this case and were never asked to justify their questions. So the time pressure when it comes, comes when us down toward the end of this indictment get up to start doing cross-examination. And I would just think -- I would just hope that you, Your Honour, and your colleagues would be somewhat sensitive to that. And that's all I can ask and that's I do ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think it ought to be said also that it was plain to me in the cross-examination of both Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Fila that they did not cross-examine anything like as exhaustively as would have been open to them. And they also have used -- I don't have an exact calculation, but I suspect they've used less time individually than you have. Now, the one thing I don't want to get down to is that sort of detailed assessment of the situation and the time that's been used. I also am taking cognisance of the fact that earlier in the case, they have not asked very many questions. And I put that down to a fact that as a group of counsel working together, you have you have agreed on who would take the lead, who was perhaps most affected, albeit you may all be affected by the evidence of particular witnesses. So I would certainly not accept that what has happened in the cross-examination of this witness is in any way unfair to you. So we will leave the matter there until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Tanic, I'm afraid you have to return again tomorrow. Be back ready to resume at 9.00. Meanwhile, please, no discussion with anyone about your evidence. Would you now leave the -- oh, sorry, we'll go into closed session while you leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
